entry.prover.body.0: A prover is a row of parts. The arrow before a part’s name says how it uses its rule: ← backwards, from the goal; → forwards, from the givens; ≡ as a rewrite, replacing one place in a sentence. Parts are numbered ①, ②, … in the order they are placed.
entry.prover.body.1: A part’s first line is its rule, marked \(R_1\), \(R_2\), …; the run report lists the board’s rules by the same marks first. The rule and the proof state on the part share their marks: the place the part acts on is framed in the state, and the part of the rule matched against it has a light tint; the other givens it matches are in violet; and the sentences it makes are in green — new goals, new givens and what a rewrite puts in. The rest of the rule is grey.
entry.prover.body.2: In a proof state each goal is marked \(\vdash_1\), \(\vdash_2\), …; the goal a part acts on by default has its mark in gold, the others in grey. Once a part is selected, the other places it could act on are dashed boxes; click one to move there. In a repeat frame, the place a rewrite takes automatically has only a light tint. A letter with a dashed gold underline (such as \(?A\)) is a sentence not yet settled. In a goal starting “⋀a.”, a is a thing taken arbitrarily. A ✓ after a goal means it is proved.
entry.prover.body.3: The run report says, step by step, what each part did: “⊢₁ ⟵ R₁” used a rule backwards, “Γ ⊢₁ ⟶ R₁” forwards, “⊢₁ ≡ R₁” rewrote, “⊢₁ ✓” copied a given and finished the goal. A part that did not apply has a hollow dashed step number, on the line of the step whose state it passed on; a small icon beside it gives the reason. Click ⓘ for what a step did. When every goal is proved, the report ends with “Q.E.D.”
entry.prover.body.4: On a phone, a part with a setting to change shows a pen at its top right; a part still waiting for its rule or its place says “Not configured”.
entry.prover.title: The prover
glossary.entries.assumption.body.0: A temporary assumption is a premise adopted for a derivation, not a claim that it is true in reality. If B is derived under A, an assumption box can discharge the dependence on A and yield \(A\to B\); other premises used by the proof remain.
glossary.entries.assumption.title: assumption
glossary.entries.automation.body.0: An automatic prover (a program such as E, Vampire or Z3) knows nothing of introduction or elimination and does one thing: negate what is to be proved, bring it with the hypotheses into , and look for a contradiction among the clauses. Isabelle’s sledgehammer hands them a goal, takes back the facts they used, and has metis prove it again in the kernel.
glossary.entries.automation.body.1: Modern SAT solvers (DPLL, CDCL) look for a contradiction among clauses too, only far better at choosing: unit propagation first, and when stuck, a learned clause and a step back.
glossary.entries.automation.title: automatic prover
glossary.entries.axiom.body.0: An axiom is a sentence taken as a starting point without proof, a rule with no premises. K: \(A\to (B\to A)\); S: \((A\to (B\to C))\to ((A\to B)\to (A\to C))\). In this prover K and S can both be proved with assumption boxes, as lemmas; a prover with axioms alone can only take them as given.
glossary.entries.axiom.title: axiom
glossary.entries.backtracking.body.0: When a step has several choices, keep them and return to the most recent remaining choice if a route fails: this is backtracking. Isabelle tactics can produce multiple results for later tactics to try; in Prolog, rule and subgoal order can also affect whether a search terminates.
glossary.entries.backtracking.title: Backtracking
glossary.entries.backward.body.0: Using a rule backwards from a goal is backward reasoning: match the goal to the rule’s conclusion and replace it with the rule’s premises. A matching rule with no premises finishes the goal.
glossary.entries.backward.title: backward reasoning
glossary.entries.beta.body.0: (fun h => b) a works out to “b with h replaced by a”: β-reduction, calling a function. In a proof, a made and at once applied is a detour; β-reduction takes it out, proving the same sentence.
glossary.entries.beta.title: β-reduction
glossary.entries.bound.body.0: A variable covered by some is a bound variable. It is only a placeholder: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) and \(\forall y.\, P(y)\) say the same thing, and renaming it changes nothing (α-equivalence).
glossary.entries.bound.title: bound variable
glossary.entries.capture.body.0: When an expression is put in for a variable, a free variable in it that lands under a quantifier of the same name is captured, and the meaning changes completely: putting y in for x in \(\forall x.\, \exists y.\, \text{Likes}(x,y)\) must not give \(\exists y.\, \text{Likes}(y,y)\). The cure is to rename the first: \(\exists y\) becomes \(\exists z\), then put y in, giving \(\exists z.\, \text{Likes}(y,z)\). Provers rename automatically when they substitute.
glossary.entries.capture.title: variable capture
glossary.entries.certificate.body.0: An outside prover is not in the kernel and may be wrong. So it need only hand over a certificate: which two clauses cancel into which, the steps traced back from \mark{bottom}. The kernel replays the certificate step by step, proving each with its own rules. Finding a proof is hard and checking one easy: the finder may be any program, and only the is trusted. Isabelle’s metis, and the tools in Lean and Coq that replay outside certificates, all work this way.
glossary.entries.certificate.title: Certificates
glossary.entries.classical.body.0: Adding double-negation elimination (from \(\lnot \lnot A\) infer A) to gives the corresponding classical logic. Together with negation introduction, it supports proof by contradiction and proves and Peirce’s law. Every classical propositional tautology is provable. Isabelle/HOL is classical; Lean can use classical principles.
glossary.entries.classical.title: Classical logic
glossary.entries.clause.body.0: Each string of “or” in the is a clause, and each item in it (a sentence or its negation) a literal. For a set of clauses to hold together, each clause needs at least one true literal. The empty clause has none and can never be true: it is \mark{bottom}.
glossary.entries.clause.title: clause
glossary.entries.cnf.body.0: First , then distribute “or” over “and” until every “or” is under the “and”s: strings of “or” joined by “and”, the conjunctive normal form. Each string of “or” is a clause. Distributing makes a sentence longer, exponentially at worst; automatic provers often use another conversion (naming parts with new letters) to avoid it.
glossary.entries.cnf.title: conjunctive normal form
glossary.entries.completeness.body.0: A system is complete for a semantics if every semantically valid proposition has a proof; this is the converse direction to . Every classical propositional has a proof, and classical first-order logic is complete for validity in all structures.
glossary.entries.completeness.body.1: Completeness is not decidability: proof enumeration can eventually find a derivation when one exists, but may not stop otherwise. It does not contradict arithmetic incompleteness: the former concerns first-order validity across structures, while the latter concerns true statements about the natural numbers and arithmetic theories satisfying specific conditions.
glossary.entries.completeness.title: completeness
glossary.entries.connective.body.0: Connectives form compound propositions from smaller ones: \mark{not} (not), \mark{and} (and), \mark{or} (or), \mark{implies} (if … then …), and \mark{iff} (if and only if). In classical propositional logic, their truth values are determined by their components, so they can be represented by logic gates.
glossary.entries.connective.body.1: Under classical truth-value semantics, these connectives can be expressed using “and” and “not”, or using “or” and “not”. The prover supplies corresponding introduction and elimination rules.
glossary.entries.connective.title: connective
glossary.entries.contradiction.body.0: A proposition false on every row of a classical truth table is a contradiction, for example “\(\text{it rains}\land \lnot \text{it rains}\)”. The prover uses \mark{bottom} as a distinguished false proposition; a contradictory formula is not necessarily syntactically identical to \mark{bottom}.
glossary.entries.contradiction.body.1: In this prover, \(\lnot A\) is defined as \(A\to \bot\). To prove \(\lnot A\), one can assume A and derive \mark{bottom}.
glossary.entries.contradiction.title: contradiction
glossary.entries.contrapositive.body.0: The contrapositive of \(A\to B\) is \(\lnot B\to \lnot A\). From “if it rains, it’s wet”, a dry ground rules out rain. The prover derives this direction using Apply and an assumption box.
glossary.entries.contrapositive.body.1: \(A\to B\) alone does not generally imply its converse \(B\to A\) or its inverse \(\lnot A\to \lnot B\); both inferences have counterexamples.
glossary.entries.contrapositive.title: contrapositive
glossary.entries.counterexample.body.0: To show a proposition is not a , one truth assignment making it false suffices; this is a counterexample. One counterexample refutes validity, but failure to find one is not by itself a proof.
glossary.entries.counterexample.body.1: For a proposition with no premises, an assignment making it false rules out a premise-free proof in a sound system. When premises are present, a counterexample must also make every premise true.
glossary.entries.counterexample.title: counterexample
glossary.entries.countermodel.body.0: To show that a conclusion does not follow, find a where the premises are true and the conclusion is false. This is a countermodel, the first-order counterpart of a . Tools such as Isabelle’s Nitpick search small scenarios for countermodels. The game’s countermodel checks use the same idea.
glossary.entries.countermodel.title: countermodel
glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.0: The Curry–Howard correspondence: a sentence is a type, and a proof of it is a program (a term) of that type. A proof of “\(A\to B\)” is a function, of “\(A\land B\)” a pair, of “\(A\lor B\)” a tagged value; \mark{bottom} is the empty type with no values, and “\(\lnot A\)” is “\(A\to \bot\)”; a proof of “\(\forall x\). …” is a function taking a thing, and a proof of “\(\exists x\). …” a thing paired with a proof about it.
glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.1: The rules used in a proof match one for one: Apply is function application, the assumption box is λ, joining and splitting are making a pair and taking a component, and cases is branching on the tag. So checking a proof is checking a type.
glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.2: Proof by contradiction has no program: none can conjure a proof of A out of “A cannot fail”. So intuitionistic logic is exactly the part programs can do, and classical logic must add proof by contradiction or excluded middle as an axiom.
glossary.entries.curry-howard.title: Curry–Howard correspondence
glossary.entries.currying.body.0: A function taking a pair and one taking its arguments one at a time can each be rewritten as the other: \(A\land B\to C\) and \(A\to (B\to C)\) give each other. Turning the first into the second is currying, named after Haskell Curry. In proof assistants functions of several arguments and rules of several premises are all written to take them one at a time.
glossary.entries.currying.title: currying
glossary.entries.decision.body.0: A program that, for every problem of a kind, stops and correctly answers yes or no is a decision procedure. Tautologies of propositional logic can be decided (work out the whole truth table); linear arithmetic and Presburger arithmetic have decision procedures too. First-order logic as a whole has none.
glossary.entries.decision.title: decision procedure
glossary.entries.declaration.body.0: In this game, a declaration specifies introduction rules for a new connective, from which the prover generates a corresponding elimination rule. This differs from an unfoldable and an assumed . The generated rule corresponds to the declared introductions; consistency also depends on the specific rules and system assumptions. Lean’s inductive types and Isabelle/HOL’s connectives have their own mechanisms; the game is a simplified model.
glossary.entries.declaration.title: Declarations
glossary.entries.deduction.body.0: The deduction theorem: if B follows from existing premises together with an additional A, then \(A\to B\) follows from the existing premises alone. It removes the dependence on A while retaining the other premises. In this game’s implicational fragment, the derivation can be rewritten using K, S and Apply.
glossary.entries.deduction.title: deduction theorem
glossary.entries.definition.body.0: A definition gives something already there a new name: a proof, a sentence, or a new kind of sentence. A definition can always be unfolded back into what it stands for, so adding one proves nothing that could not be proved before; an axiom is different, it states something new. Packing a proof into a part defines a lemma: in Lean, theorem chain := … is such a definition, and Isabelle too keeps each proved theorem under its name.
glossary.entries.definition.title: definition
glossary.entries.demorgan.body.0: \(\lnot (A\lor B)\) is equivalent to \(\lnot A\land \lnot B\), and \(\lnot (A\land B)\) to \(\lnot A\lor \lnot B\): a negation passing through “or” becomes “and”, and through “and” becomes “or”. Quantifiers too: \(\lnot \forall x.\, P(x)\) is equivalent to \(\exists x.\, \lnot P(x)\), and \(\lnot \exists x.\, P(x)\) to \(\forall x.\, \lnot P(x)\). Two of the directions, \(\lnot (A\land B)\to \lnot A\lor \lnot B\) and \mark{not}\mark{forall} \mark{implies} \mark{exists}\mark{not}, take proof by contradiction.
glossary.entries.demorgan.title: De Morgan
glossary.entries.dep-function.body.0: A proof of “\(\forall x.\, P(x)\)” is a function whose argument is not a proof but a thing: give it t and it gives back a proof of P(t). The type of the result varies with the argument, so it is a dependent function, its type written Π x, P x, in Lean simply \mark{forall} x, P x. \mark{exists} corresponds to the dependent pair (Σ type): a thing, and a proof that it fits.
glossary.entries.dep-function.title: dependent function
glossary.entries.dfs.body.0: Following one path to its end (done, or stuck) before going back for the next is depth-first search. It saves space, remembering only the current path; the price is that it may follow an endless path forever. So automatic tactics often bound the depth, or deepen it a level at a time.
glossary.entries.dfs.title: depth-first search
glossary.entries.diagonal.body.0: Lay out a table of x against y, look only at the diagonal of x against x, and flip every cell of it: what you get differs from every row of the table. This is the diagonal argument (Cantor, 1891). The barber, a set with more subsets than members, a machine rejecting its own code: each is the on a table.
glossary.entries.diagonal.title: diagonal argument
glossary.entries.dsyll.body.0: From \(A\lor B\) and \(\lnot A\), B: this is the disjunctive syllogism, the process of elimination. In the prover it is no rule of its own but a case split: the A side meets \(\lnot A\) in \mark{bottom}, which goes to ; the B side is the conclusion already.
glossary.entries.dsyll.title: disjunctive syllogism
glossary.entries.elim-rule.body.0: An elimination rule explains how to use a proposition with a : A follows from \(A\land B\); B follows from \(A\to B\) and A; and \(A\lor B\) supports reasoning by cases. Using a proposition in a proof does not consume it. Harmony requires elimination rules to correspond appropriately to the ways that connective is introduced.
glossary.entries.elim-rule.title: elimination rule
glossary.entries.equality.body.0: a = b says two names stand for one thing. It has two rules: everything equals itself (reflexivity); and when a = b, what holds of a holds of b (substitution). Symmetry and transitivity are proved from these two.
glossary.entries.equality.body.1: Equations serve as rewrite rules too: the simplifier uses a = b to replace a with b in a sentence. By the chapter on proof terms, a = b is a type itself.
glossary.entries.equality.title: Equality
glossary.entries.equivalence.body.0: In classical propositional logic, A and B are semantically equivalent if they have the same truth value under every assignment. The biconditional \(A\leftrightarrow B\) states both implications and can be written \((A\to B)\land (B\to A)\).
glossary.entries.equivalence.body.1: Equivalent sentences can stand in for each other: replace any part of a sentence with something equivalent and the whole keeps its truth. This is what the simplifier relies on to turn a sentence into another way of saying the same.
glossary.entries.equivalence.title: equivalence
glossary.entries.explosion.body.0: From a \mark{bottom} anything can be proved: the rule is often called the principle of explosion (Latin ex falso quodlibet). In the prover it is the part .
glossary.entries.explosion.body.1: In classical truth-value semantics, a conditional with a false antecedent is true. The prover instead applies contradiction elimination to derive the desired conclusion from \mark{bottom}; this does not mean contradictory premises are true in reality.
glossary.entries.explosion.title: principle of explosion
glossary.entries.fol.body.0: A letter in propositional logic stands for a whole proposition. First-order logic also describes internal structure: names denote objects, predicates express properties or relations, and \mark{forall} and \mark{exists} mean “for all” and “there exists”.
glossary.entries.fol.body.1: “First-order” means that quantifiers range over objects in the domain, not over predicates or properties. It can express “everyone is mortal”; quantifying over all properties requires a higher-order language.
glossary.entries.fol.title: First-order logic
glossary.entries.forward.body.0: Using a rule forwards from the givens is forward reasoning: read the rule’s premises from the givens and add its conclusion to them. The new statements can be used later in the proof.
glossary.entries.forward.title: forward reasoning
glossary.entries.free.body.0: A variable not bound by a relevant quantifier is free. The truth of P(x), for example, depends on a structure and an assignment to x. Treating the free variable as an unknown turns the formula into a query.
glossary.entries.free.title: free variable
glossary.entries.hilbert.body.0: A prover whose one rule is , all else being taken as an , is a Hilbert system: for the “if … then …” part of propositional logic, the axioms K and S are enough. Its proofs are hard to write, with no assumption box and every step assembled from axioms; the topic Without the box proves in such a system.
glossary.entries.hilbert.title: Hilbert system
glossary.entries.intro-rule.body.0: An introduction rule has a new in its conclusion: Join gets \(A\land B\) from A and B, Choose gets \(A\lor B\) from A, the assumption box gets \(A\to B\). To prove a sentence, its outermost connective says which introduction rule to use.
glossary.entries.intro-rule.title: introduction rule
glossary.entries.intuitionistic.body.0: Intuitionistic logic does not adopt double-negation elimination or as a general principle. It proves \(\lnot \lnot (A\lor \lnot A)\), but not excluded middle for arbitrary A without premises. For a premise-free disjunction theorem, the disjunction property ensures that at least one disjunct is provable; proofs from premises can also reason by cases.
glossary.entries.intuitionistic.title: intuitionistic logic
glossary.entries.isabelle.body.0: Isabelle (Paulson, from 1986) takes the LCF road: a theorem is an abstract type thm, and only a few functions in the kernel (one per rule of inference) can make one, with no proof term to keep. Its most used logic, HOL, is classical higher-order logic. Rules are written \mark{open-bracket}premises\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion, each in them filled in by unification, and tactics and the simplifier put rules together to use them automatically; sledgehammer calls on outside automatic provers.
glossary.entries.isabelle.title: Isabelle
glossary.entries.kernel.body.0: The kernel checks proofs against basic rules. Lemmas, tactics and simplifiers can help construct a proof, but their results must still be checked by the kernel.
glossary.entries.kernel.body.1: A smaller kernel is easier to audit. Trust in a checked result still depends on the chosen axioms, the kernel implementation and its execution environment.
glossary.entries.kernel.title: The kernel
glossary.entries.lambda.body.0: fun h => b (also written λ h => b) makes a function: given an h, give b. This is λ-abstraction, as written in Church’s λ-calculus of the 1930s. The assumption box is λ: its assumption is the parameter h, its proof the body b, and outside comes a proof of \(A\to B\).
glossary.entries.lambda.title: λ-abstraction
glossary.entries.lcf.body.0: LCF (Milner, from 1972) set a design: a theorem is an abstract type only the kernel can make, and tactics are ordinary programs that make theorems only by calling the kernel’s rules. So however intricate a or clever the automation, none of it need be trusted, only the kernel. To write tactics Milner invented the language ML. Isabelle, HOL4 and HOL Light all descend from it.
glossary.entries.lcf.title: LCF
glossary.entries.lean.body.0: Lean (de Moura, from 2013) is built on dependent type theory. Every proof written ends up as a proof term, and the kernel checks that its type is the sentence to prove. The terms are kept, so anyone can recheck them with another checker: the de Bruijn criterion. Lean’s logic is intuitionistic at heart, classical reasoning coming from the axiom Classical.em; the mathematics library mathlib is written in it.
glossary.entries.lean.title: Lean
glossary.entries.lem.body.0: The law of excluded middle \(A\lor \lnot A\) states that A or its negation holds. It is a classical propositional tautology, but has no premise-free proof using this game’s intuitionistic rules alone. Adding double-negation elimination makes it provable; the result becomes <part-ref to="lemma:lem"></part-ref>.
glossary.entries.lem.body.1: <wiki-ref to="classical"></wiki-ref> accepts excluded middle; <wiki-ref to="intuitionistic"></wiki-ref> does not adopt it as a general principle.
glossary.entries.lem.title: Excluded middle
glossary.entries.lemma.body.0: A lemma is a proved result that can be reused in later proofs. For example, packages the inference from \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\) to \(A\to C\). Its validity rests on its proof and permitted substitutions, not merely on test examples; unfolding it traces the proof back to the rules.
glossary.entries.lemma.title: lemma
glossary.entries.liar.body.0: “This sentence is false”: if it is true it is false, and if false, true. The island’s version is “I am a knave”, which nobody can say. It is no flaw of logic but a tool: let something speak of itself and say the opposite, and it proves that a thing cannot exist. Russell’s paradox, Cantor’s theorem and the halting problem are all of it.
glossary.entries.liar.title: The liar
glossary.entries.metavariable.body.0: The letters of a rule stand for any sentence. When a rule is used backwards those letters are not yet settled; they are metavariables, written ?A and ?B, with ?t for any thing and ?P(x) for any sentence about x. Unification fills them in. Isabelle also writes the letters of a proved theorem as ?A (in its metalogic Pure, \mark{entails} is “yields” and \mark{meta-all} “for any”); the holes ?m Lean’s apply leaves are metavariables too.
glossary.entries.metavariable.title: metavariable
glossary.entries.mgu.body.0: A solution of is a unifier. The most general unifier settles only what must be settled and leaves every other metavariable open; every other unifier can be had from it by substituting further. When first-order unification has a solution it has a most general one, unique up to renaming.
glossary.entries.mgu.title: most general unifier
glossary.entries.motive.body.0: In Lean, a = b is a type too. The only way to make one is rfl (a = a), and the only way to use one is Eq.rec, written h ▸ p: h proves a = b and p a sentence about a, giving that sentence with some of its a’s replaced by b. Which ones is said by a function fun x => …, the motive; Lean can usually read it off the sentence to prove. Symmetry and transitivity are built from these two: h ▸ rfl, k ▸ h.
glossary.entries.motive.title: motive
glossary.entries.natural.body.0: Natural deduction organizes reasoning by : introduction rules establish propositions with that connective, and elimination rules derive consequences from them. For example, \mark{and} has conjunction introduction and elimination, \mark{implies} has the assumption box and Apply, and \mark{bottom} has .
glossary.entries.natural.body.1: Natural deduction organizes proofs using temporary assumptions and inference steps. Proof assistants can express rules in similar forms, though their kernels and rule systems differ.
glossary.entries.natural.title: natural deduction
glossary.entries.nnf.body.0: A sentence with no \mark{implies} or \mark{iff}, and every \mark{not} on a smallest sentence, is in negation normal form. Turn \(A\to B\) into \(\lnot A\lor B\), drop double negations, and push each \mark{not} all the way in with : every sentence comes to this shape, meaning the same.
glossary.entries.nnf.title: negation normal form
glossary.entries.normal-form.body.0: Take the detours (brought in, then at once used up) out of a proof term one by one until none is left, and what remains is the normal form. Every proof term of intuitionistic logic comes to a normal form, the same whichever detour goes first (strong normalisation and confluence). A normal proof uses only what appears in the sentence it proves, the starting point of Gentzen’s and Prawitz’s proof theory.
glossary.entries.normal-form.title: normal form
glossary.entries.pattern.body.0: A metavariable followed by variables (?P(x)) makes higher-order, which in general has more than one solution and is not even decidable. Miller found that when a metavariable is followed only by distinct bound variables (a higher-order pattern), there is one solution: ?P is the function with those variables as its parameters. Isabelle and Lean rely on pattern unification day to day; what is not a pattern waits to be settled elsewhere.
glossary.entries.pattern.title: higher-order pattern
glossary.entries.predicate.body.0: A predicate says what one or more things are or how they relate: “… is human”, Human(x), takes one; “… is a parent of …”, Parent(x, y), takes two. A predicate filled with things makes a sentence: whether Human(h) is true depends on whether h is human in the scenario.
glossary.entries.predicate.title: predicate
glossary.entries.proof-state.body.0: The goals still open, each with what it has to work from, are the proof state. A proof starts with a single goal, every rule used changes the state, and when no goal is left it is done. In Isabelle a proof state is itself a theorem \mark{open-bracket}subgoals\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} goal, one premise fewer for each subgoal proved; in Lean it is a set of metavariables still to fill.
glossary.entries.proof-state.title: proof state
glossary.entries.proof-term.body.0: A proof written as an expression is its proof term: a given is a name, Apply is p q, the assumption box fun h => …, Join ⟨a, b⟩. By the , it is a program as well, whose type is the sentence it proves. A proof term kept can be checked again by anyone with another checker.
glossary.entries.proof-term.title: proof term
glossary.entries.proof.body.0: A proof is a finite derivation from premises, axioms and inference rules. Each step is an allowed starting point or follows from earlier steps by a rule; checking rule applicability depends on formula structure.
glossary.entries.proof.body.1: A propositional truth table grows exponentially in the number of atoms. A formal proof can use general rules and variables to establish a family of cases; reasoning about infinite domains still requires appropriate quantifiers and rules.
glossary.entries.proof.title: Proof
glossary.entries.provers.body.0: A proof assistant is a program in which a person and the machine write proofs together, every step checked by the machine. Each has a small : only the kernel can declare a theorem proved, and however clever the automation around it, everything goes through the kernel, so it cannot make a false theorem.
glossary.entries.provers.body.1: This game’s prover is built that way from its first part: a kernel of a few rules, and lemmas proved with them. It borrows only proof assistants’ way of building a kernel and its parts; its own parts and notation are fitted to the game.
glossary.entries.provers.title: Proof assistants
glossary.entries.quantifier.body.0: A quantifier says for how many things a sentence holds: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) says every x has P, \(\exists x.\, P(x)\) that at least one does. x is a variable standing for “any one”, and the quantifier reaches over everything after it.
glossary.entries.quantifier.body.1: In classical logic, \(\lnot \forall x.\, P(x)\) is equivalent to \(\exists x.\, \lnot P(x)\); the forward direction generally requires classical reasoning. Quantifier order matters too: \(\forall x.\, \exists y.\, \text{Likes}(x,y)\) does not imply \(\exists y.\, \forall x.\, \text{Likes}(x,y)\).
glossary.entries.quantifier.title: quantifier
glossary.entries.query.body.0: A sentence with a free variable is a query. In a given scenario, its answers are the things that make the sentence true when substituted for the variable. SQL and Datalog use the same idea: a table corresponds to a predicate, and its rows list the values that satisfy it.
glossary.entries.query.title: query
glossary.entries.recursor.body.0: When an inductive type is declared, Lean’s kernel checks its constructors (its s) and then makes its recursor, its : one case for each constructor, the constructor’s type with its conclusion put as any motive (R here). And.rec, Or.rec and False.rec come of it so; Isabelle’s conjE and disjE have the same shape. A recursor also comes with a rule of computation: met with a constructor, it computes on (ι-reduction).
glossary.entries.recursor.body.1: Why the elimination rule can only be so: a declaration says “these are the only ways”, and the elimination rule writes that as a rule. It gives no more (introduce, then eliminate, is a detour that can always be taken out: what the rule hands back is what was handed in), and no less (take apart and put together, and the sentence is back). Proof theory calls this the harmony of introduction and elimination. If elimination rules could simply be written, one could write Prior’s tonk: introduced as “or”, eliminated as “and”, proving anything at all.
glossary.entries.recursor.title: recursor
glossary.entries.reduction.body.0: If A can be solved with a solver for B, A reduces to B. If A is undecidable, so is B: otherwise B’s decision procedure, with the reduction, would decide A. This is how spreads from one problem to a whole chain of others.
glossary.entries.reduction.title: reduction
glossary.entries.reflection.body.0: Reflection keeps no certificate: write the sentences to decide as data, write a , prove once that it is right, and after that every problem needs only the kernel to run the program, the proof term being rfl. Lean’s decide and Coq’s ssreflect take this road. How fast depends on how the kernel computes, so some decision procedures (Lean’s omega, say) produce a proof for the kernel to check instead.
glossary.entries.reflection.title: reflection
glossary.entries.refutation.body.0: When a set of clauses is unsatisfiable, is sure to reach the empty clause from it: refutation completeness. It does not promise to prove every sentence directly, only to find the contradiction when denying it is one, which is just enough: to prove C, show \(\lnot C\) contradicts the hypotheses. When it stops without \mark{bottom}, the clauses can all hold at once.
glossary.entries.refutation.title: refutation completeness
glossary.entries.resolution.body.0: Take a literal A in one and \(\lnot A\) in another, cancel the pair and join what is left with “or”: that is resolution (Robinson, 1965). Only one pair goes at a time. When the clauses have variables, the pair undergoes first. Reaching the empty clause is reaching \mark{bottom}.
glossary.entries.resolution.title: Resolve
glossary.entries.rewrite.body.0: \(l\longmapsto r\) is a rewrite rule: a place in a sentence that fits the left side l is replaced by the right side r. It rests on l and r giving each other (equivalence), or on l = r. A rule may carry a condition, and the rewrite is right only once the condition is proved. A set of rules used to the end must make the sentence “simpler” each time, or it goes round in circles.
glossary.entries.rewrite.title: rewrite rule
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.0: Every rule in the game is written \mark{open-bracket}premises\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion, the way Isabelle writes it: \mark{open-bracket}it rains; it’s windy\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} it rains \mark{and} it’s windy says “\(\text{with proofs of it rains and it’s windy},\text{you have a proof of it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\)”. In a rule, the letters A and B stand for any sentence and R for any conclusion.
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.1: The double arrow \mark{entails} and the single arrow \mark{implies} are not on one level. \mark{implies} is inside a sentence: \(A\to B\) is itself a sentence, which can be proved, assumed and wired into other parts. \mark{entails} is outside sentences and relates proofs: with these, you have that. The kernel joins them: the assumption box turns “assume A, prove B” into a sentence \(A\to B\), and Apply goes back, from \(A\to B\) and A to B. Isabelle keeps the two levels apart: \mark{entails} belongs to its meta-logic Pure, \mark{implies} to the logic HOL.
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.2: Lean has one arrow. A way to make is written And.intro : a → b → a ∧ b: a rule is an implication, and the way to make is its proof (the Curry–Howard correspondence), so a rule is applied just as a sentence with \mark{implies} is. The two notations say one thing: \mark{open-bracket}A; B\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} C is \(A\to B\to C\).
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.3: When writing a declaration in the game, only the outermost layer of \mark{entails} is written: an intro rule is “\mark{open-bracket}premise; premise\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion”, each premise a whole sentence; a premise that needs premises of its own says so inside its sentence, with \mark{implies} and \mark{forall}, as in \mark{open-bracket}\(\forall y.\, y\) below \(x\to y\) reachable\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} x reachable. So writing a declaration and writing a lemma take one format: one conclusion, a few intro rules, each a row of premises side by side, with whatever is complex kept inside the statements. Isabelle’s own way writes that inner layer as a rule too, \mark{open-bracket}\mark{meta-all}y. \mark{open-bracket}y below x\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} y reachable\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} x reachable, so that the kernel splits it into subgoals when the rule is used, with no for-any box and assumption box needed first to prove a sentence with \mark{implies}. The two can be turned into each other and say the same; the game takes the first so the rules a player writes have one format and read simply. The elimination rule made from them still follows Isabelle, its premises with premises and things of their own: the kernel writes it, not the player. Lean has one arrow and writes intro rules as a constructor’s arguments, nearer the game’s way.
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.title: the rule arrow \mark{entails}
glossary.entries.rule.body.0: An inference rule specifies how conclusions follow from premises. For example, Apply derives B from \(A\to B\) and A. Letters represent proposition schemata and can be consistently instantiated as the rule permits. In a proof, a rule part’s inputs represent premises and its output represents the conclusion.
glossary.entries.rule.title: rule of inference
glossary.entries.satisfiable.body.0: A sentence (or several together) is satisfiable when it is true in at least one scenario. If none makes it true, it is a , also called unsatisfiable. In propositional logic, a scenario is a row of the . In first-order logic, it also specifies the things, what names refer to, and when predicates hold.
glossary.entries.satisfiable.body.1: In classical propositional logic, A is a tautology exactly when \(\lnot A\) is unsatisfiable. Refutation-based methods negate the goal and check whether a satisfying assignment remains.
glossary.entries.satisfiable.title: satisfiability
glossary.entries.scripts.body.0: Isabelle’s Isar (Wenzel, from 1999) writes proofs as text for people, a structured proof: have proves a sentence on the way, show the one wanted, assume, fix and obtain bring in an assumption, an arbitrary thing and a thing taken out, and proof … qed is a block. The method after each by does one small step, and the system checks every row. Lean writes much the same: have h : A := by …, show B, intro, obtain ⟨x, h⟩ := …, and calc for a chain of equations.
glossary.entries.scripts.body.1: A script, a proof term and a proof circuit are one proof: each row a part, each block a box. Large formalisations (the four colour theorem, the Kepler conjecture, the libraries mathlib and the AFP) are written this way: people write the structure and the lemmas, automation fills in the small steps.
glossary.entries.scripts.title: Structured proofs
glossary.entries.simplifier.body.0: A simplifier takes a set of rules, each a , and replaces wherever one fits in a sentence, until none fits. Each rule is a proved equivalence or equation, so every step is accepted by the kernel. Isabelle’s and Lean’s simp are such programs, the automation used most every day.
glossary.entries.simplifier.title: The simplifier
glossary.entries.skolem.body.0: Clauses hold only “for all”. In \(\forall x.\, \exists y.\, P(x,y)\), y varies with x, so it is replaced by a new function sk(x): \(\forall x.\, P\)(x, sk(x)). This is Skolemisation. The result is not equivalent to the original, but it is satisfiable exactly when the original is, which is all a search for a contradiction needs.
glossary.entries.skolem.title: Skolem function
glossary.entries.soundness.body.0: A rule is sound if its conclusion is true whenever all its premises are true. To refute an inference, a counterexample must make all premises true and the conclusion false.
glossary.entries.soundness.body.1: The corresponding completeness property says that every semantically valid conclusion has a formal proof. Both properties are relative to a particular system and semantics; completeness does not imply a terminating decision procedure.
glossary.entries.soundness.title: soundness
glossary.entries.tactic.body.0: A tactic is a program that turns a into new ones. It can only change it a rule at a time, so however intricate tactics get, what they prove goes through the kernel. Isabelle’s auto and Lean’s simp and omega are tactics.
glossary.entries.tactic.body.1: Tactics can be combined: run them in sequence or repeatedly, or let later steps work on candidate results.
glossary.entries.tactic.title: Tactics
glossary.entries.tautology.body.0: A proposition true on every row of its is a tautology, for example “\(\text{it rains}\to \text{it rains}\)” or “\(\text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it rains}\)”. Consistently substituting propositions for its atoms preserves validity.
glossary.entries.tautology.body.1: A complete truth table decides whether a propositional formula is a tautology, but n atoms require 2ⁿ rows. A proof instead derives its conclusion using rules, without enumerating each row.
glossary.entries.tautology.title: tautology
glossary.entries.theorem.body.0: A theorem is a proposition proved without undischarged premises. An assumption box discharges one specified temporary assumption; the result is premise-free only when all other dependencies are discharged too. In a sound classical propositional system, theorems are instances; a corresponding complete system proves every tautology.
glossary.entries.theorem.title: theorem
glossary.entries.truth.body.0: A compound proposition is built from atoms and connectives such as “if … then …” and “and”. In classical propositional logic, its value is determined by the values of its atoms. A truth table lists every assignment and result: n distinct atoms give 2ⁿ assignments.
glossary.entries.truth.body.1: The conditional \(X\to Y\) is false only when X is true and Y false. When its antecedent X is false, the conditional is true by definition. This connective is material implication; it does not assert that X causes Y.
glossary.entries.truth.title: truth table
glossary.entries.undecidable.body.0: When no decision procedure answers every problem of a kind correctly, the kind is undecidable. The halting problem was the first (Turing, 1936). First-order validity is undecidable too, only semi-decidable (Church and Turing, 1936): what follows, a methodical search always finds; on what does not, the search may never stop. So automation can help, but never do it all.
glossary.entries.undecidable.title: undecidability
glossary.entries.unification.body.0: Unification solves equations \(s\doteq t\): it finds what to put in for each so that both sides become the same. First-order unification is solved by a few rules (Martelli and Montanari’s form: decompose, delete, clash, swap, occurs check, eliminate). Robinson invented it in 1965 for resolution proofs; it became the heart of Prolog, type inference and proof assistants.
glossary.entries.unification.title: Unification
glossary.entries.unit.body.0: A clause with one literal (a unit clause) states a forced fact; with it makes another clause one literal shorter. Passing such facts along is unit propagation. For Horn clauses (at most one literal without \mark{not} each) it is enough, and fast; SAT solvers do it first at every step.
glossary.entries.unit.title: unit propagation
glossary.entries.vacuous.body.0: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\to Q(x)\) holds when nothing satisfies P, true without checking anything: a vacuous truth. “All his children are at school” holds for someone with no children; that is right in logic, but in a query it is often not what was meant, and “has children” must be added.
glossary.entries.vacuous.title: vacuous truth
glossary.entries.world.body.0: In first-order logic, a scenario (also called a structure or model) specifies what things there are, what each name refers to, and which things satisfy each predicate. These settings determine whether a sentence is true.
glossary.entries.world.body.1: A sentence that is always true holds in every scenario. There are infinitely many scenarios, so checking them one by one cannot replace a proof.
glossary.entries.world.title: scenario
level.always.after: Whether a proposition is a tautology depends only on its logical form: put other propositions in place of its atoms and the verdict stays the same.
level.always.intro.0.t: “If X, then Y” is written \(X\to Y\); “X and Y” is true only when both X and Y are.
level.always.intro.1.t: A proposition true on every row is a <wiki-ref to="tautology"></wiki-ref>.
level.always.tasks.always.brief: Which of these five propositions are true on every row? Mark each one.
level.always.tasks.always.hint.0: If you are unsure, expand the truth table and check its rows.
level.always.tasks.always.hint.1: One false row is enough to rule it out.
level.always.tasks.always.hint.2: “If it rains and it’s windy, then it’s wet”: can it rain and be windy while the ground stays dry?
level.always.title: Always true
level.and.after: A sentence proved from no givens is a <wiki-ref to="theorem"></wiki-ref>: a tautology of the truth tables, here proved.
level.and.intro.0.t: In the prover, “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\)” means what the <part-ref to="part:gAnd"></part-ref> gate of <level-ref to="g-and"></level-ref> does: it rains, and it’s windy.
level.and.intro.1.t: <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref> declared “and”, and two parts became available for proofs: <part-ref to="part:andI"></part-ref>, its one introduction rule, and <part-ref to="part:andE"></part-ref>, the elimination rule made from it, whose two outputs give the left and the right. Every connective has its introduction and elimination rules; a system of rules organised this way is called <wiki-ref to="natural"></wiki-ref>.
level.and.tasks.and-1.hint.0: Compare the given with the goal. What has changed about the two sides of “and”?
level.and.tasks.and-2.hint.0: The goal is a conditional. How does its condition relate to the given in the previous task?
level.and.tasks.and-2.intro.0.t: This time nothing is given: “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\to \text{it’s windy}\land \text{it rains}\)” always holds.
level.and.title: Proving and
level.assume.intro.0.t: How can we prove “if A, then B”? We can temporarily assume A and prove B under that condition. An <wiki-ref to="assumption"></wiki-ref> is a starting point for reasoning; it does not assert that A already holds.
level.assume.intro.1.t: The <part-ref to="part:impI"></part-ref> represents this reasoning with a box. Choose A as the assumption on the part and it becomes available inside. Connect the B proved inside to “Conclusion”, and the box gives \(A\to B\) outside.
level.assume.intro.2.t: Outside the box, the temporary assumption A is no longer a given. The conclusion says that if A holds, B follows; any other givens used in the proof still remain.
level.assume.tasks.assume-1.hint.0: What follows the “if” in the goal?
level.assume.tasks.assume-1.hint.1: From inside the box, the givens on the board are visible.
level.assume.tasks.assume-2.hint.0: How many \mark{implies}s are in the goal?
level.assume.tasks.assume-2.intro.0.t: A box can sit inside a box. The inner one sees the outer one’s assumption and the givens on the board.
level.assume.title: Assumption
level.au-adder.after: Formal verification in chip design checks circuits in this spirit.
level.au-adder.intro.0.t: A circuit can be written as equivalences, one per output wire against its inputs: the sum bit is “exactly one input is 1”, the carry bit “both inputs are 1”. A property of the circuit is whatever follows from them.
level.au-adder.tasks.au-adder.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that follow and reports failure for the rest.
level.au-adder.tasks.au-adder.hint.0: Compare the circuit properties in the cases. Which follow from the definitions of sum and carry?
level.au-adder.title: Half adder
level.au-cert.after: Finding a proof is hard; checking one is easy.
level.au-cert.intro.0.t: The saturator makes dozens of clauses, and \mark{bottom} needs only a few. Tracing \mark{bottom} back through where each clause came from gives a <wiki-ref to="certificate"></wiki-ref>: which two cancel into which.
level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that derives \mark{bottom} and produces a resolution certificate.
level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert-1.hint.0: Look at the run result. Which clauses record where they came from?
level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert-2.briefNote: Rebuild the proof from the proof assistant’s certificate.
level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert-2.hint.0: Each clause in the certificate names the two it came from.
level.au-cert.title: Certificate
level.au-clauses.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="au-skolem"></level-ref> prepared the sentences among the givens. The new part “Into clauses” extracts <wiki-ref to="clause"></wiki-ref> from a proof state whose goal is \mark{bottom}; the wire then carries clauses.
level.au-clauses.tasks.au-clauses.brief: Design a proof assistant that produces the required clauses for each case.
level.au-clauses.tasks.au-clauses.hint.0: Look at the required clauses. In what form does the original goal appear?
level.au-clauses.tasks.au-clauses.hint.1: In the quantified cases, which names appear in the required clauses?
level.au-clauses.title: Clauses
level.au-horn.after: In a SAT solver this is called <wiki-ref to="unit"></wiki-ref>.
level.au-horn.intro.0.t: Each round the saturator cancels every pair, and most new clauses go unused. In these clauses each has at most one literal without \mark{not}: they are Horn clauses.
level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.brief: Design a proof assistant that derives \mark{bottom} within each test’s clause limit.
level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.hint.0: Some clauses have a single literal from the start.
level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.hint.1: A one-literal clause is something already forced.
level.au-horn.title: Forced facts
level.au-iff.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="sp-simp"></level-ref>, a given equivalence helped rewrite sentences. Equivalence itself can also be expressed in another form. Here you will prove the relationship between the two.
level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff-1.hint.0: How do the two parts of the goal relate to the given equivalence?
level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff-2.hint.0: How do the two sides of the given “and” relate to the two directions in the goal?
level.au-iff.title: Forms of iff
level.au-machine.intro.0.t: You built proofs by hand earlier. This time, hand the goals to the prover.
level.au-machine.tasks.au-machine.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that follow and reports failure for the rest.
level.au-machine.tasks.au-machine.hint.0: Compare the givens and goals across the cases. Which goals follow from the givens?
level.au-machine.title: Auto proof
level.au-negate.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="lemma:auto"></part-ref> applies rules one at a time, and its search can slow down on larger goals. Another kind of <wiki-ref to="automation"></wiki-ref> proves goals by looking for contradictions. Isabelle’s Sledgehammer sends goals to provers of this kind.
level.au-negate.tasks.au-negate.brief: Design a proof assistant that turns each goal into \mark{bottom}, with the negation of what was to be proved among the hypotheses.
level.au-negate.tasks.au-negate.hint.0: Compare the original goal with the extra given in each required result. How are they related?
level.au-negate.title: Seeking a conflict
level.au-onepair.intro.0.t: “Resolve” refuses when two pairs could cancel. “\(\text{It rains}\lor \text{it’s windy}\)” and “\(\lnot \text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it’s windy}\)” hold two: cancel both at once and nothing is left, as if a contradiction followed. Why not cancel both?
level.au-onepair.tasks.au-onepair.brief: Find a row of the truth table where “\(\text{it rains}\lor \text{it’s windy}\)” and “\(\lnot \text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it’s windy}\)” are both true.
level.au-onepair.tasks.au-onepair.hint.0: Can rain and wind have the same truth value when both sentences are true?
level.au-onepair.title: One pair
level.au-refute.intro.0.t: The empty clause has no literal in it, nothing that could be true: it is the contradiction \mark{bottom}.
level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute-1.hint.0: “It rains” is itself a clause of one literal.
level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute-2.brief: Now prove \mark{bottom} from “\(I\; \text{take the bus}\lor I\; \text{cycle}\)”, “\(\lnot I\; \text{take the bus}\lor I\; \text{arrive on time}\)”, “\(\lnot I\; \text{cycle}\lor I\; \text{arrive on time}\)” and “\(\lnot I\; \text{arrive on time}\)”.
level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute-2.hint.0: Two copies of the same literal merge into one.
level.au-refute.title: Empty clause
level.au-replay.after: In Isabelle, proofs found by Sledgehammer are likewise replayed in the kernel by metis.
level.au-replay.intro.0.t: The new part “Replay” hands the certificate to the kernel: each clause used must really come out of a hypothesis, and each step must be proved by <part-ref to="lemma:auto"></part-ref> from the two it came from. If all pass, the goal the clauses came from is proved.
level.au-replay.tasks.au-replay.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.au-replay.tasks.au-replay.hint.0: Look at the run result. Where do the certificate and proof state appear?
level.au-replay.title: Proof replay
level.au-resolve.intro.0.t: Between clauses one rule is enough. One clause has “it rains”, the other “\mark{not}it rains”: rain or not, one of them still holds with that literal taken away.
level.au-resolve.tasks.au-resolve.hint.0: How do the parts about rain in the two givens relate?
level.au-resolve.tasks.au-resolve.hint.1: When it rains, and when it does not, which part of the goal holds?
level.au-resolve.title: Resolution
level.au-saturate.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="au-refute"></level-ref> you chose which pair to cancel at each step. A proof assistant does not choose: the new part “Resolution round” cancels every pair that can be cancelled, once, adding each new clause along with the two it came from. When clauses have variables, a pair of literals is unified first, then cancelled: “\(\lnot x\; \text{is human}\lor x\; \text{is mortal}\)” and “Socrates is human”, with x unified to Socrates.
level.au-saturate.tasks.au-saturate.brie: Design a proof assistant that resolves until it derives \mark{bottom} or no new clauses appear.
level.au-saturate.tasks.au-saturate.hint: After one round, the new clauses may still have pairs to cancel.
Compare the clauses produced in the first round with the final result. What remains after one round?
level.au-saturate.title: Saturation
level.au-skolem.after: Skolemising does not keep the hypotheses equivalent, only satisfiable together or not at all: they are equisatisfiable.
level.au-skolem.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="au-negate"></level-ref>, the sentences needed to look for a contradiction became givens. These givens have different forms, and some contain quantifiers. They now need a form suitable for working with clauses.
level.au-skolem.intro.1.t: Clauses contain no existential quantifiers. For example, in “everyone has a parent”, the parent depends on the person. The new part “Skolemise” can express this dependence with a <wiki-ref to="skolem"></wiki-ref>, such as sk1(x) for the parent of x. It handles existential quantifiers in negation normal form.
level.au-skolem.tasks.au-skolem.brief: Design a proof assistant that transforms the givens in each case into the required form.
level.au-skolem.tasks.au-skolem.hint.0: In the run result, how have the givens changed while the goal remains \mark{bottom}?
level.au-skolem.tasks.au-skolem.hint.1: In the “everyone has a parent” case, which quantifier is associated with sk1(x) in the result?
level.au-skolem.title: Existence and ties
level.au-sledge.after: A \mark{bottom} reached by the proof assistant is vouched for by nothing but itself: the clauses were not proved by the kernel.
level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that starts from the goal and resolves until it derives \mark{bottom} or no new clauses appear.
level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-1.hint.0: Compare the starting goals with the input the saturator receives. What differs?
level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-2.brief: Find a row where the hypotheses all hold and the goal does not.
level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-2.hint.0: Look at the one-literal clauses after saturating.
On the last goal, the proof assistant saturated without reaching \mark{bottom}.
level.au-sledge.title: Prover
level.au-wrong.after: Outside provers fall within the <wiki-ref to="lcf"></wiki-ref> design too: only the kernel need be trusted.
level.au-wrong.intro.0.t: Someone hands over a prover said to be far faster than the saturator: it cancels every opposite pair two clauses share, all at once. It is on the board already, and it reaches \mark{bottom} on every goal.
level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that replays the external certificate in the kernel and identifies the error.
level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong-1.hint.0: Compare the external prover’s certificate with the replay result. Which step fails?
level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong-2.brief: Find a row showing the first goal really does not follow: the hypotheses hold, the goal does not.
The kernel would not take the first goal’s certificate.
level.au-wrong.title: Wrong proof
level.bot.after: Once the givens contradict each other, everything can be proved, and true can no longer be told from false.
level.bot.intro.0.t: A witness says “the door is locked”, then “the door is not locked”. Both cannot be true.
level.bot.intro.1.t: You met a in : a sentence false on every row. Here we write falsity as \mark{bottom}.
level.bot.intro.2.t: <part-ref to="part:botE"></part-ref> is the elimination rule of \mark{bottom}: from \mark{bottom} it proves whichever sentence is chosen on the part. This is <wiki-ref to="explosion"></wiki-ref>.
level.bot.tasks.bot-1.hint.0: Compare the two givens about the door. What would the other given imply if the door were locked?
level.bot.tasks.bot-1.hint.1: The goal is about the moon. Which given conflicts with the door being locked?
level.bot.tasks.bot-2.hint.0: Compare the condition in the goal with the given. Can both hold?
level.bot.tasks.bot-2.intro.0.t: In a truth table, an “if … then …” is true whenever its “if” part is false. Here the rules prove one instance of it.
level.bot.title: A conflict
level.box.intro.0.t: On a Saturday, if it rains I rest at home. It is raining.
level.box.tasks.box.hint.0: What follows the “if” in the goal?
level.box.tasks.box.hint.1: Click the empty space inside the box first, and the parts you place next land in it.
level.box.title: Eliminate a condition
level.byContra.intro.0.t: “Suppose the door is not locked; that leads to a contradiction; so it is locked.” This is proof by contradiction.
level.byContra.tasks.byContra.hint.0: Compare the givens. Do they have the same condition? How are their conclusions related?
level.byContra.tasks.byContra.hint.1: When would these givens produce opposite conclusions at the same time?
level.byContra.title: Indirect proof
level.c-arrow.intro.0.t: “If it rains, it’s wet” and “it does not rain, or it’s wet” say the same: each is false only on the row where it rains and the ground is dry.
level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow-1.hint.0: The given does not say whether it rains.
level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow-2.hint.0: How does the condition in the goal relate to one side of the given “or”?
level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow-2.hint.1: Compare the two cases in the given with the condition and conclusion of the goal.
level.c-arrow.title: If–then
level.c-contra.intro.0.t: The <wiki-ref to="contrapositive"></wiki-ref> of “if A then B” is “if not B then not A”. This time the other way: from the contrapositive back to the sentence.
level.c-contra.tasks.c-contra.hint.0: Compare the condition and conclusion of the given with the two sentences in the goal.
level.c-contra.tasks.c-contra.hint.1: If it rains and the ground is not wet, what does the given imply?
level.c-contra.title: Back to the if
level.c-dist.intro.0.t: “It rains, or it’s windy and wet” and “it rains or is windy, and it rains or is wet” say the same: “or” distributes over “and”, as multiplication does over addition. With the “and” on the right and on the left, that makes two pairs, four directions.
level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist-1.hint.0: How do the two “or” statements in the goal relate to the two cases in the given?
level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist-2.hint.0: What do the two “or” statements in the given share?
level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist-2.hint.1: If the shared part does not hold, how do the remaining parts relate to the goal?
level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist-3.hint.0: Compare the position of “and” in the given and goal with the first task.
level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist-4.hint.0: Which part of the goal is shared by the two “or” statements?
level.c-dist.title: Distribution
level.c-dneg.intro.0.t: Two sentences that each give the other say the same thing: they are in <wiki-ref to="equivalence"></wiki-ref>. “\mark{not}\mark{not}it rains” and “it rains” are such a pair.
level.c-dneg.intro.1.t: Once both directions are proved, they make one part that switches between the two.
level.c-dneg.tasks.c-dneg-1.hint.0: Compare the given and goal. How many negations does each have?
level.c-dneg.tasks.c-dneg-2.hint.0: What does the goal deny, and how does that relate to the given?
level.c-dneg.title: Double negation
level.c-either.intro.0.t: If it rains I take the bus; if not, I cycle. I do not know whether it will rain, but it will be one or the other.
level.c-either.tasks.c-either.hint.0: How do the conditions of the givens relate to the two sides of the goal?
level.c-either.tasks.c-either.hint.1: Which side of the goal holds when it rains, and when it does not?
level.c-either.title: Bus or bicycle
level.c-wall.intro.0.t: These five sentences are true on every row of their truth tables. How many does <part-ref to="lemma:auto"></part-ref> prove?
level.c-wall.intro.1.t: A search that finds no proof does not show there is none: the method or the depth may fall short.
level.c-wall.tasks.c-wall.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals auto can handle and reports failure for the rest.
level.c-wall.tasks.c-wall.hint.0: Try each with the <part-ref to="lemma:auto"></part-ref> you have, and see which it cannot prove.
level.c-wall.title: Auto limits
level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.0: What do the bus and bicycle cases have in common in the sentence to be proved?
level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.1: Look at the two case boxes. Which given conditional relates to each assumption?
level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.2: Compare the conclusions of the two boxes with the goal. Do they say the same thing?
level.chain.after: A proved result kept for reuse is a <wiki-ref to="lemma"></wiki-ref>. Such a part is only a name for a proof, a <wiki-ref to="definition"></wiki-ref>, and adds nothing to what can be proved.
level.chain.intro.0.t: A proof, once wired, can be kept as a part and used from then on without opening a box. First, a part for each of a few moves that come up all the time.
level.chain.intro.1.t: If it rains, it’s wet; if it’s wet, it’s slippery. So if it rains, it’s slippery. One step by instinct, but the kernel has no such rule.
level.chain.tasks.chain.hint.0: The goal is “if it rains, then …”.
level.chain.title: Chain
level.contra.intro.0.t: “If it rains, it’s wet”, so “if it isn’t wet, it did not rain”. This is the <wiki-ref to="contrapositive"></wiki-ref>, and unlike the bad reasoning of <level-ref to="onerow"></level-ref> it always holds: “\((\text{it rains}\to \text{it’s wet})\to (\lnot \text{it’s wet}\to \lnot \text{it rains})\)”.
level.contra.tasks.contra.hint.0: How many nested conditionals are in the goal? What is the condition in each?
level.contra.tasks.contra.hint.1: Compare “it is not wet” with “if it rains, it is wet”. Which sentence would rain conflict with?
level.contra.tasks.mt-1.hint.0: Compare the two conditionals with “the road is not slippery”. What lies between rain and a slippery road?
level.contra.tasks.mt-1.intro.0.t: Rain wets the ground, a wet ground is slippery; the road is not slippery, so it did not rain.
level.contra.tasks.mt-2.brief: Find a row that makes “\((\text{it rains}\to \text{it’s wet})\to (\lnot \text{it rains}\to \lnot \text{it’s wet})\)” false.
level.contra.tasks.mt-2.hint.0: Look at the outermost “if … then …”. Which truth values would make it false?
level.contra.tasks.mt-2.hint.1: Could it not rain, and the ground still be wet?
level.contra.tasks.mt-2.intro.0.t: “Rain makes the ground wet, so no rain, no wet ground.” This too negates both sides, only without swapping them. Does it follow? Look for a counterexample first.
level.contra.title: If not
level.copy.intro.0.t: Every new atomic sentence doubles the rows in a truth table. The prover’s <wiki-ref to="kernel"></wiki-ref> takes a different approach: start from the premises and derive the conclusion one step at a time.
level.copy.intro.1.t: The givens on the left are the premises; the goal on the right is the proposition to prove. A wire carries a sentence already proved.
level.copy.intro.2.t: The cases put different sentences in place of the letters of one pattern. The general form shows the letters themselves. One board must pass every test.
level.copy.tasks.copy.hint.0: A given’s dot is on its right; the goal’s dot is on its left.
level.copy.title: Copy
level.curry.intro.0.t: “If it rains and it’s windy, it’s wet” and “if it rains, then if it is also windy, it’s wet” say the same.
level.curry.tasks.curry-1.hint.0: The goal has two “if … then …”s, one inside the other.
level.curry.tasks.curry-1.hint.1: Compare the “and” in the given condition with the two conditions in the goal. Which sentences do they share?
level.curry.tasks.curry-2.hint.0: Compare the goal’s condition with the two conditions in the given. Where do Saturday and rain appear?
level.curry.title: Conditions
level.decl-and.after: “And” was not in the kernel before; the declaration is what makes the kernel know it. You may have noticed the <wiki-ref to="elim-rule"></wiki-ref> written under the rule table, generated from the introduction rules: the declaration lists all the ways to construct the statement, so using it means considering each of those ways. Lean takes this road of declaring: “and”, “or”, “there is” and equality each come into its kernel by a declaration (inductive), and their rules are generated from it; only “if … then …” is built into Lean’s kernel.
level.decl-and.intro.0.t: So far the kernel knows only “if … then …” (\mark{implies}): the <part-ref to="part:impI"></part-ref> proves it and <part-ref to="part:mp"></part-ref> uses it, both built into the kernel. A kernel does not automatically know new symbols: in dependent type theory, a <wiki-ref to="declaration"></wiki-ref> can specify how a new symbol is constructed and used. Now the kernel is to know a new connective, “and”: both statements hold.
level.decl-and.intro.1.t: A rule is written “\mark{open-bracket}premises\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion”: if its premises hold, the conclusion follows. The <wiki-ref to="rule-arrow"></wiki-ref> connects the premises and conclusion of a rule; \mark{implies} means “if … then …” within a statement.
level.decl-and.intro.2.t: An <wiki-ref to="intro-rule"></wiki-ref> says how to prove a statement with a connective, an <wiki-ref to="elim-rule"></wiki-ref> how to use it. The assumption box is the introduction rule of “if … then …”, Apply its elimination rule. A declaration writes the introduction rules; the kernel makes the elimination rule.
level.decl-and.intro.3.t: “Derivable from” lists the premises needed for the conclusion. Select “Add a premise” to enter each one. If there are several ways to derive the conclusion, select “Add a row” and enter the premises for each way.
level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.brief: Write a declaration that meets the requirement.
level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.hint.0: Look at the requirement. What does it require of each sentence in the conclusion?
level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.hint.1: Compare the premises under “Derivable from” with the requirement. Would introduction still be allowed if one were missing?
level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.say: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved.
level.decl-and.title: Declare And
level.decl-bot.after: The elimination rule of \mark{bottom} has no case to handle, so once \mark{bottom} is held, every goal is derivable: the principle of explosion. “Not” comes from contradiction too: \(\lnot A\) is defined as \(A\to \bot\), “if A held, it would lead to a contradiction”. So with A and \(\lnot A\) both as premises, Apply gives \mark{bottom}, and from it any statement follows.
level.decl-bot.intro.0.t: A contradiction is a situation that cannot hold, such as “it rains” and “it does not rain” holding together. Once reasoning reaches a contradiction, the premises it rests on cannot all hold.
level.decl-bot.intro.1.t: The kernel writes a contradiction as the statement \mark{bottom}. \mark{bottom} never holds, so its declaration has no introduction rule at all: no premises are enough to prove it. The board holds that declaration.
level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.brief: Following the declaration, fill in whether each case’s conclusion is derivable.
level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.hint.0: \mark{bottom} has no introduction rule. Under which premises can it be introduced?
level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.hint.1: The elimination rule asks for each introduction rule to be considered in turn. With none, what is left to consider?
level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.say: \mark{bottom} never holds: no premises are enough to prove it.
level.decl-bot.title: Declare False
level.decl-check.after: Test cases can show a declaration wrong; they cannot show it right.
level.decl-check.intro.0.t: A test case checks whether a declaration captures the intended meaning. Each case describes a situation: the available premises, the goal, and whether the goal is expected to follow from those premises.
level.decl-check.intro.1.t: A declaration specifies which derivations are allowed. When a test runs, the prover gives a result according to the declaration and compares it with the expectation. A mismatch shows that the declaration does not capture the intended meaning in that situation.
level.decl-check.intro.2.t: In this level, first write a case that agrees with your own declaration, then find a case that disagrees with another declaration, and last check one declaration in two directions.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-1.brie: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Find a situation where the expectation meets the requirement and the declaration’s result agrees with it.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-1.hint: Choose the premises and the conclusion first, then ask what the requirement says: should the conclusion be derivable?
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-1.intr: The table holds your declaration from <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref>. Find a situation in which its result agrees with your expectation, and enter it in the table.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-2.brie: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Find a situation where the expectation meets the requirement but the declaration’s result disagrees with it.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-2.hint: Does this declaration ask for the same premises as the requirement?
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-2.intr: The table now holds someone else’s declaration. Find a situation in which its result disagrees with your expectation, and enter it in the table.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-3.afte: From the introduction direction alone this declaration shows no fault: with “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\)”, “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\)” of course holds. But the extra rule gives the elimination rule one more case, which hands back nothing, so “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\)” alone no longer yields “it rains”. One harmless-looking extra intro rule may show its fault only in use, so both directions must be checked.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-3.brie: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Complete case 2 to reveal this declaration’s fault from the use direction.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-3.hint: This declaration’s elimination rule has two cases. What does the second give back from “\(A\land B\)”?
By the requirement, what follows from “\(A\land B\)” alone?
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check-3.intr: A declaration is checked from two directions. The introduction direction takes the declared statement as the goal and checks under which premises it can be obtained; the use direction puts it among the premises and checks what follows from it. The intro rules decide the first direction; the elimination rule generated from them decides the second.

The declaration on the table has one intro rule too many: from “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\)”, introduce “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\)”. Case 1 is already written and checks the introduction direction: the result agrees with the expectation. In fact this declaration passes every case written from this direction.
level.decl-check.title: Declaration check
level.decl-equiv.intro.0.t: In the truth circuits, the \mark{iff} of <level-ref to="g-iff"></level-ref> meant true together and false together. In the kernel, \(A\leftrightarrow B\) is “\((A\to B)\land (B\to A)\)”: the \mark{implies} holds both ways.
level.decl-equiv.tasks.decl-iff-2.brief: Write a declaration that meets the requirement.
level.decl-equiv.tasks.decl-iff-2.hint.0: Does the requirement need both at once, or is either enough?
A premise need not be a single letter; it can be a sentence with \mark{implies} in it, built with the connective in the premise window. A rule is written with one layer of \mark{entails}; whatever a premise needs in turn goes inside its sentence.
level.decl-equiv.tasks.decl-iff-2.say: “\(A\leftrightarrow B\)” may be introduced only when the “if … then” both ways are proved.
level.decl-equiv.title: Declare iff
level.decl-ex.intro.0.t: “For all” needs no declaration: proved for any thing taken, it is proved for all, and the kernel can already do that. “There is” is different: “\(\exists y.\, y\) is human” needs some thing and a proof that it is human, such as “Socrates is human”.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-eq.after: This introduction rule is reflexivity; the elimination rule of equality is substitution.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-eq.brief: Write a declaration that meets the requirement.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-eq.hint.0: What do the two sides of an “s = t” proved from nothing have in common?
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-eq.intro.0.t: Are the Morning Star and the Evening Star one star? To say two things are equal, equality has to be declared first.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-eq.say: Everything equals itself; two different names cannot be proved equal from nothing.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-1.brief: Write test cases whose expectations meet the requirement but whose results under the declaration disagree with them.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-1.hint.0: Having taken a thing, which sentence about it does this declaration ask for?
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-1.hint.1: Which sentence about that thing does this declaration’s elimination rule hand back? By the requirement, does the same follow from “\(\exists y.\, P(y)\)” alone?
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-1.intro.0.t: The declaration on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-1.say: “\(\exists y.\, P(y)\)” may be introduced once some thing is proved to satisfy P.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-2.brief: Write a declaration that meets the requirement.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-2.hint.0: The introduction rule needs two things: a thing, and a sentence about it.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-2.hint.1: How is the arbitrary name related to the premise in the introduction rule?
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-2.intro.0.t: Each row now starts with a switch, “for any x”: turned on, the rule holds for any thing x taken, and its premises may mention x.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-2.say: “\(\exists y.\, P(y)\)” may be introduced once some thing is proved to satisfy P.
level.decl-ex.title: Declare exists, equality
level.decl-iff.intro.0.t: “If and only if” makes one sentence of the “if … then” both ways.
level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-1.brief: Requirement: “\(A\leftrightarrow B\)” may be introduced only when the “if … then” both ways are proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-1.hint.0: Does each of this declaration’s two introduction rules need one thing or two?
level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-1.hint.1: With “\(A\leftrightarrow B\)”, what follows from “B” by the requirement? What does each case of this declaration’s elimination rule hand back?
The declaration of “if and only if” on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
level.decl-iff.title: Declare Iff
level.decl-or.intro.0.t: In truth circuits, an “or” is true when at least one side holds, including when both hold. Does the declaration on the board match that meaning?
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-1.brief: Write test cases whose expectations meet the requirement but whose results under the declaration disagree with them.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-1.hint.0: With “\(A\lor B\)” at hand, does the requirement let you conclude “A”?
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-1.say: “\(A\lor B\)” may be introduced once either “A” or “B” is proved.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-3.after: The elimination rule made from the intro rules of “or” is what is usually called reasoning by cases.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-3.brief: Write a declaration that meets the requirement.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-3.hint.0: Compare the case where only A is proved with the case where only B is proved. What does the requirement say about their conclusions?
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-3.say: “\(A\lor B\)” may be introduced once either “A” or “B” is proved.
level.decl-or.title: Declare Or
level.decl-order.after: Test cases see only what can be derived, not how a rule is written; the kernel keeps to the rule written down.
level.decl-order.intro.0.t: The “and” of <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref> takes “it rains” first, then “it’s windy”. Would the other order do? Can test cases tell?
level.decl-order.intro.1.t: Declaration 1 takes “it rains” first, declaration 2 “it’s windy” first. Write a case for each direction, introduction and use, expected derivable, and check both declarations.
level.decl-order.tasks.decl-order-2.brie: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both agree.
level.decl-order.tasks.decl-order-2.hint: Does the order of the premises change what introducing “and” needs?
level.decl-order.tasks.decl-order.brief: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both agree.
level.decl-order.tasks.decl-order.hint.0: What does introducing “and” need? What can be taken out of an “and”?
level.decl-order.title: Order
level.decl-strength.intro.0.t: A declaration can be wrong on either side: too strong, failing to introduce when it should; too weak, introducing when it should not. Both faults show from the introduction and the use direction alike.
level.decl-strength.tasks.decl-strength-: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
What does “and” need, by the requirement? What does this declaration’s intro rule ask for?

The table holds someone else’s declaration of “and”. Its introduction conditions are too strong: premises that should be enough to prove an “and” statement are not enough under this declaration. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to expose its fault.
