Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
How much does each of this declaration’s intro rules need? How much does “and” need, by the requirement?
The table now holds another declaration of “and”. This time its introduction conditions are too weak: it accepts premises that should not be enough to prove an “and” statement.
A declaration determines both when “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it’s windy}\)” can be introduced and what follows from it. Again write a test case for each direction to expose the error.
level.decl-strength.title: Strength
level.decl-three.intro.0.t: “And” and “or” each join two sentences. Here there are three.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-1.brie: Requirement: “\(A\land (B\land C)\)” may be introduced only when “A”, “B” and “C” are all proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-1.hint: How many introduction rules does this declaration have, and what does each need?
Into how many cases does the elimination rule made from it split, and what does each case hand back?
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-1.intr: The declaration on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-2.afte: The more introduction rules, the easier to introduce and the harder to use: each one more is one more case to handle when taking it apart.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-2.brie: Requirement: “\(A\lor (B\lor C)\)” may be introduced once any one of “A”, “B”, “C” is proved. Following this declaration, fill in whether each case’s conclusion is derivable.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-2.hint: To derive a sentence from “one of three”, each of the three cases must derive it on its own.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-2.intr: The board holds the declaration of “one of three”: three introduction rules, each needing one thing.
level.decl-three.title: Three items
level.decl-true.after: True is often written \mark{top}, the very opposite of \mark{bottom}: knowing it holds tells you nothing more.
level.decl-true.intro.0.t: The opposite of \mark{bottom}: True always holds. The table holds its declaration: one intro rule with no premises, needing nothing.
level.decl-true.tasks.decl-true.brief: Requirement: True needs nothing: it may be introduced whatever is at hand, even with nothing at all. Following this declaration, fill in whether each case’s conclusion is derivable.
level.decl-true.tasks.decl-true.hint.0: This declaration’s elimination rule has one case, which hands back nothing.
level.decl-true.title: Declare True
level.decl-two.after: “Exactly one agrees” cannot be declared, though: an introduction rule can say what makes a sentence, never what stops it.
level.decl-two.intro.0.t: What is declared need not be a connective: whatever holds in ways that can be spelled out can be declared.
level.decl-two.intro.1.t: The declaration of “the motion passes” on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.brief: Requirement: “the motion passes” may be introduced only when at least two of “A”, “B”, “C” are proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.hint.0: How many pairs can be taken from the three? Which does this declaration write out?
level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.hint.1: Which sentence is in every one of this declaration’s introduction rules?
level.decl-two.title: Two items
level.demorgan.intro.0.t: “Neither Saturday nor Sunday” and “not (Saturday or Sunday)” say the same; so do “not (Saturday and Sunday)” and “not Saturday, or not Sunday”. These are <wiki-ref to="demorgan"></wiki-ref>.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-1.hint.0: Which day does each negation in the goal concern?
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-1.hint.1: The given denies “Saturday or Sunday”. What if one side holds?
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-2.hint.0: Compare the two negations in the given with the “or” in the goal.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-2.hint.1: Which part of the goal does each negation in the given concern?
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-3.hint.0: Which part of the goal is denied by each case in the given?
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-3.hint.1: Compare the two cases in the given with the two parts of “and” in the goal.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-4.hint.0: The given does not say which one fails.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-4.hint.1: What would Saturday and not Saturday each mean for the goal?
level.demorgan.title: De Morgan
level.drinker.after: It sounds absurd, yet it is a theorem of classical logic: the proof says such a person exists without saying who.
level.drinker.intro.0.t: There is at least one person in the pub. “\(\exists x.\, x\) is drinking \mark{implies} \(\forall y.\, y\) is drinking” says: there is someone such that, if they drink, everyone drinks.
level.drinker.tasks.drinker.hint.0: What condition must the person in the goal satisfy?
level.drinker.tasks.drinker.hint.1: Compare the cases where everyone drinks and where someone does not.
level.drinker.title: Drinker
level.e-count.after: Only one row lights up: a is a knight, b and c are knaves. “At least one” is a string of “or”s; “at most one” is an “or” for every pair, joined by “and”; “not the only one” is a string of “or”s too. Problems such as rostering (at least so many on duty, at most so many on leave at once, someone who may not work alone) are put to a SAT solver the same way: each counting phrase rewritten as strings of “or”s, joined together.
level.e-count.intro.0.t: “At least”, “at most” and “only” speak of how many, and and, or and not have no gate that counts. Such words must first be said another way, as a sentence about whether each person is a knight.
level.e-count.tasks.e-count.brief: a says: “At least one of the three of us is a knave.” b says: “At most one of the three of us is a knave.” c says: “a is not the only knight.” Translate what the three say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.0: “At least one is a knave”: of the three, who might that knave be?
level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.1: “At most one knave” means no two people are knaves at once. Pick any two people: what must be true of them?
level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.2: “a is not the only knight”: either a is not a knight, or there is another knight.
level.e-count.title: Counting knights
level.e-one.tasks.e-one.brief: a says: “At least one of us two is a knave.” Translate this into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what a says fits what a is.
level.e-one.tasks.e-one.hint.0: Translate what a says first, then “a says”.
level.e-one.tasks.e-one.hint.1: “a is a knave” is “a is not a knight”.
level.e-one.title: One islander
level.e-says.after: Both could be knights, or both could be knaves. This clue leaves two possibilities. In the next puzzles, you’ll use the same method to check more complicated statements.
level.e-says.intro.0.t: You arrive on an island and meet two residents, a and b. Every islander is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies.
level.e-says.intro.1.t: a speaks first. Put “a is a knight” and what a says into one formula, then use the truth table to find the identities that fit the island’s rules.
level.e-says.tasks.e-says-translate.brie: Use the cards to express how a’s identity must relate to this clue.
level.e-says.tasks.e-says-translate.hint: If a is a knight, the statement must be true. What if a is a knave?
Which connective requires both sides to have the same truth value?
level.e-says.tasks.e-says.brief: Wire your formula and run the truth table. Find the rows where a’s statement fits a’s identity.
level.e-says.tasks.e-says.hint.0: Use the two knight-status inputs for the two propositions in your formula, then connect them with the corresponding gate.
level.e-says.title: Island talk
level.e-three.after: Finding a row on which several sentences are all true is the <wiki-ref to="satisfiable"></wiki-ref> problem (SAT).
level.e-three.intro.0.t: Three people, and the table has eight rows.
level.e-three.tasks.e-three.brief: a says: “b is a knave.” b says: “c is a knave.” c says: “a and b are both knaves.” Translate what the three say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
level.e-three.tasks.e-three.hint.0: In what c says, which part does the negation cover?
level.e-three.tasks.e-three.hint.1: Translate each person’s words on their own; all three must hold at once.
level.e-three.title: Three islanders
level.e-two.tasks.e-two.brief: a says: “b is a knave.” b says: “We are both knights.” Translate what both say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
level.e-two.tasks.e-two.hint.0: Translate what each person says on its own.
level.e-two.title: Two islanders
level.e-words.after: All four rows are false. The rule says rain makes the ground wet, so it cannot hold alongside a report of rain leaving the ground dry. A formula that is false on every row is a <wiki-ref to="contradiction"></wiki-ref>. Its truth value matches \mark{bottom}, and the circuit is now available as the Contradiction part.
level.e-words.intro.0.t: You can wire a simple sentence directly. With a longer sentence, it’s easy to lose track of what each gate should connect. Translate the sentence into a logical formula first, then use the formula to guide your wiring.
level.e-words.intro.1.t: Practice translating a short sentence, then try a more complicated rain report. In the circuit, use the basic claims as inputs and turn the connectives into gates. The truth table runs the circuit once for each combination of inputs.
level.e-words.tasks.e-words-translate.br: Use the cards to build a formula for this log.
level.e-words.tasks.e-words-translate.hi: Start with “If it rains, the yard gets wet”. Which connective expresses that condition?
The second sentence says it rained and the ground stayed dry. Join the two sentences with another And.
level.e-words.tasks.e-words-translate.sa: The log says: “If it rains, the yard gets wet. It rained, but the yard stayed dry.”
level.e-words.tasks.e-words-warmup.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
The sentence says both that it’s raining and that it’s wet. Which connective requires both claims to be true?
level.e-words.tasks.g-always-2.brief: Wire the formula you just built. Run the truth table and see whether any row makes both claims in the report true.
level.e-words.tasks.g-always-2.hint.0: Revisit Translate the report to check your formula. Wire the inner connectives first, then feed their outputs into the outer ones.
level.e-words.title: Rain report
level.fo-all.intro.0.t: The universal \mark{forall} reads “for all”: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) says every thing x in the scenario satisfies P.
level.fo-all.intro.1.t: First translate the sentence into a formula. If the checker finds a scenario where one is true and the other is false, it shows that scenario. Then construct a scenario yourself to check someone else’s translation.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.hint.0: Suppose there is just one thing. What does the sentence require if it is human? What if it is not?
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.hint.1: Writing “\(x\; \text{is human}\land x\; \text{is mortal}\)” says every thing in the scenario is human.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.after: A sentence that always holds is true in every scenario. There are infinitely many scenarios, with no bound on how many things they can contain.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.brief: Construct a scenario in which the two sentences differ in truth.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.hint.0: Tap “is human” under a thing to make it human; tap again to undo.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.hint.1: What does this translation require of every thing? What if one thing is not human?
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.intro.0.t: In propositional logic, the truth of a sentence depends on the row of the truth table. In first-order logic, it depends on the <wiki-ref to="world"></wiki-ref>: how many things there are, what properties they have, and how they relate.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.intro.1.t: To check the two translations, set how many things the scenario has, then light up the properties under each thing. A run marks each translation true or false beside it.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-1.brief: Use cards to write the premises and the conclusion of the argument.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-1.hint.0: Find the premises and conclusion of the argument, then count the sentences in the premise.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-1.intro.0.t: An argument has premises and a conclusion. Write them separately on the declaration board, then construct a scenario to test whether the conclusion follows.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-1.say: Every human is mortal. Socrates is mortal. Therefore Socrates is human.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-2.after: A scenario where the premises are true and the conclusion is false is a <wiki-ref to="countermodel"></wiki-ref>.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-2.brief: Construct a scenario where every premise is true and the conclusion is false.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-2.hint.0: Must the name Socrates refer to a human?
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-2.intro.0.t: A run checks each premise and the conclusion on the rule board in the scenario you build. If every premise is true and the conclusion is false, the scenario is a counterexample.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-2.intro.1.t: Each name refers to one thing: tap “Socrates” under a thing to make the name refer to it.
level.fo-all.tasks.m-counter-2.say: Every human is mortal. Socrates is mortal. Therefore Socrates is human.
level.fo-all.title: For all
level.fo-atoms.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-atoms.intro.0.t: In propositional logic a letter stands for a whole sentence: saying whether each person is mortal takes a letter per person, and “everyone” or “someone” cannot be said at all.
level.fo-atoms.intro.1.t: takes sentences apart: a name stands for a thing, and a says what a thing is or how things relate. “Socrates is human” is written Human(h), “Ann likes Bo” Likes(i, j): the order of the places matters.
level.fo-atoms.intro.2.t: To translate a sentence, first find what joins its parts. “Yet” works like “and”, and “either … or …” works like “or”. You can restate both “as long as” and “only if” as “if … then …”. Which part is enough to conclude the other? No proofs for the next few levels: first learn how to write a sentence and tell whether it is true in a scenario.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-1.hint.0: Which word joins the two halves of the sentence?
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-1.hint.1: Who occupies each place in the parent relation? Which half is negated?
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-1.say: Ann is a parent of Bo, yet Bo does not like Ann.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-2.hint.0: How many possibilities does the sentence mention? Does it rule either one out?
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-2.say: Socrates is either a bird or human.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-3.hint.0: Which two parts does “only if” connect?
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-3.say: Ann likes Bo only if Bo is human.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-as-long-as: Restate the sentence as “if … then …”. Which part follows “if”?
As long as Bo is human, Ann likes Bo.
level.fo-atoms.title: Translation
level.fo-nested.intro.0.t: A quantifier may hold another. Each has its own variable and reaches over everything after it: in \(\forall x\). … \(\exists y\). …, x and y each stand for their own thing. A variable some quantifier covers is a <wiki-ref to="bound"></wiki-ref>; one no quantifier covers is a <wiki-ref to="free"></wiki-ref>, and then the sentence does not say whom it means.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-1.hint.0: Who likes whom in the sentence? Can the two places use the same name?
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-2.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-2.hint.0: Whose parent is involved? How many things does the sentence mention?
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-3.brief: Construct a scenario in which the two sentences differ in truth.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-3.hint.0: Think of it as a game: the opponent picks for \mark{forall}, you pick for \mark{exists}. In the first, the opponent picks x first, then you pick y; in the second you pick y first, then the opponent picks x.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-3.hint.1: Try different liking relations in a small scenario. When is each sentence true or false?
An arrow from one thing to another says the first likes the second. Tap a thing, then tap what it likes (itself included) to draw an arrow; tap an arrow to erase it.
level.fo-nested.title: Nested scope
level.fo-some.intro.0.t: A new symbol, \mark{exists}, reads “there exists”: \(\exists x.\, P(x)\) says at least one thing x in the scenario satisfies P.
level.fo-some.intro.1.t: First translate the sentence into a formula. If the checker finds a scenario where one is true and the other is false, it shows that scenario. Then construct a scenario yourself to check someone else’s translation.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.hint.0: What must exist for the sentence to be true? Which conditions must it satisfy?
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.hint.1: Writing “\(x\; \text{is a bird}\to x\; \text{flies}\)” is made true by anything at all that is not a bird.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.brief: Construct a scenario in which the two sentences differ in truth.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.hint.0: Consider a scenario with no birds. Is each translation true or false?
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.intro.0.t: In propositional logic, the truth of a sentence depends on the row of the truth table. In first-order logic, it depends on the <wiki-ref to="world"></wiki-ref>: how many things there are, what properties they have, and how they relate.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.intro.1.t: To check the two translations, set how many things the scenario has, then light up the properties under each thing. A run marks each translation true or false beside it.
level.fo-some.title: Something exists
level.g-always.after: The sentence is true on every row: it is a <wiki-ref to="tautology"></wiki-ref>. Its truth value matches \mark{top}, and the circuit is now available as the Always True part.
level.g-always.intro.0.t: An Implies gate has a direction. If you join the two directions with Or, which rows can come out false?
level.g-always.tasks.g-always-1.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “‘if it rains, it’s wet’ or ‘if it’s wet, it rains’” on every row.
level.g-always.tasks.g-always-1.hint.0: Wire “it rains” and “it’s wet” into the two Implies gates in opposite orders.
level.g-always.title: Always true
level.g-and.intro.0.t: A truth table is filled in row by row. Wire a circuit once and the machine runs it on every row. Select a row to see each part’s value.
level.g-and.intro.1.t: The new part <part-ref to="part:gAnd"></part-ref> outputs true only when both inputs are true.
level.g-and.tasks.g-and.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “It rains and it is windy” on every row.
level.g-and.tasks.g-and.hint.0: The sentence holds only when both rain and wind are present.
level.g-and.title: And
level.g-iff.after: When both directions hold, the inputs have matching truth values. This is <wiki-ref to="equivalence"></wiki-ref>, written \mark{iff}. The circuit you built is now available as the “Equivalent” gate.
level.g-iff.intro.0.t: Earlier, Or required at least one direction to hold. Now use And to require both directions and see what happens to the output.
level.g-iff.tasks.g-iff.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “‘if it rains, it’s wet’ and ‘if it’s wet, it rains’” on every row.
level.g-iff.tasks.g-iff.hint.0: Compare the two input columns. Find the rows where their values match.
level.g-iff.title: Equivalence
level.g-imp.after: With the condition and result swapped, the new claim is false only when it’s wet and it didn’t rain. Input order matters for an Implies gate.
level.g-imp.intro.0.t: Remember the forecast in <level-ref to="table"></level-ref>? “If it rains, it’s wet” is false only when it rains and the ground stays dry. The conditional is true whenever it doesn’t rain or it’s wet.
level.g-imp.tasks.g-imp-2.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “if it’s wet, it must have rained” on every row.
level.g-imp.tasks.g-imp-2.hint.0: Wire the condition that follows “if” into the first input of the Implies gate.
level.g-imp.tasks.g-imp.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “it isn’t raining or it’s wet” on every row.
level.g-imp.tasks.g-imp.hint.0: Wire “it’s wet” straight into Or. Only “it rains” goes through Not first.
level.g-imp.title: Implies
level.g-not.intro.0.t: A truth table is filled in row by row. A <wiki-ref to="logic/circuit"></wiki-ref> is wired once, and the machine runs it on every row.
level.g-not.intro.1.t: “It rains” on the left gives its value on the current row; “The sentence” on the right takes the board’s output.
level.g-not.intro.2.t: The new part stands for negation, \mark{not}: true in gives false out, false in gives true out.
level.g-not.intro.3.t: Select a row of the truth table to see each part’s value on that row.
level.g-not.tasks.g-not.brief: Wire a board that works out the value of “it is not the case that it is not raining” on every row.
level.g-not.tasks.g-not.hint.0: How is “it is not raining” wired? And negated once more?
level.g-not.title: Not
level.g-or.after: Or needs at least one true input. The gate still outputs true when it’s both raining and windy.
level.g-or.intro.0.t: “It rains or it’s wet” is false only when there’s no rain and the ground is dry. Build that behavior with the gates you have, then pack the circuit into an Or gate.
level.g-or.tasks.g-or-2.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “it’s raining or it’s windy” on every row.
level.g-or.tasks.g-or.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “it’s not the case that ‘it isn’t raining and the ground is dry’” on every row.
level.g-or.tasks.g-or.hint.0: Feed the And output into the last Not gate, then wire its output to “The sentence”.
level.g-or.title: Or
level.g-tree.after: “It is windy but not raining” requires wind and no rain. “Rain and wind did not occur together” rules out only their occurring together. The scope of the negation changes the truth value.
level.g-tree.intro.0.t: A sentence can deny one thing, or deny that two things happen together. Wire each sentence and compare their truth tables.
level.g-tree.tasks.g-tree-together.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “Rain and wind did not occur together” on every row. Compare the two truth tables.
Which combination of rain and wind does this sentence rule out?
level.g-tree.tasks.g-tree.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “It is windy but not raining” on every row.
level.g-tree.tasks.g-tree.hint.0: What does the sentence say about rain and about wind?
level.g-tree.title: Scope
level.g-xor.after: The circuit outputs true only when exactly one input is true. You can now reuse it as the XOR \mark{xor} gate.
level.g-xor.tasks.g-xor.brief: “Either it rains or it’s windy, but not both.” Wire a board that computes it, with at most 4 gates.
level.g-xor.tasks.g-xor.hint.0: No need to part it together row by row. Read the sentence as it is said: what parts is it made of?
level.g-xor.title: XOR
level.h-and-make.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref> brought “and” into the kernel by a declaration. Another way declares nothing and uses the \mark{implies} and quantifier already there: “A and B” is “for every sentence R, if R follows from A and B, then R”, written \mark{forall}R. \((A\to (B\to R))\to R\).
level.h-and-make.intro.1.t: This \mark{forall} ranges not over things but over sentences. The same two parts handle it: choose the upper-case R on the <part-ref to="part:allI"></part-ref>, and inside it R is any sentence at all; in <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> choose not a thing but a sentence, to put in for R.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make-1.hint: What can R stand for in the goal?
How many layers of conditions are in the sentence inside the box?
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make-2.afte: R may be any sentence, even the very “A and B” being defined. Only because that is allowed can the definition be written at all. Isabelle/HOL takes this road: “and” and “or” are not declared but defined this way, with \mark{implies} and \mark{forall}, and their rules proved from the definitions.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make-2.hint: What kind of sentence can replace R in the definition?
After replacing R, what is the condition in the resulting sentence?
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make-2.intr: The definition holds for every sentence R, so pick one that serves.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-eq-subst.after: This is <part-ref to="part:rewrite"></part-ref>: the definition writes down equality’s elimination rule directly.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-eq-subst.hint.0: When using <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref>, what can replace P in the definition?
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-eq-subst.hint.1: Where do the Morning Star and Evening Star occur in the property in the goal?
Above, the quantifier ranged over sentences. <level-ref to="decl-ex"></level-ref> declared equality in the kernel; equality can also be defined using a quantifier: “a = b” means “every property of a is also a property of b”, written \mark{forall}P. \(P(a)\to P(b)\). Here the quantifier ranges over properties.
Given the Morning Star = the Evening Star, written out by the definition. <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> puts in a sentence about x for P: each P(t) becomes that sentence with t in place of x.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-eq-sym.after: The two ways of representing equality give the same rules.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-eq-sym.brief: Given the Morning Star = the Evening Star (by the definition), prove the Evening Star = the Morning Star (by the definition too).
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-eq-sym.hint.0: In the definition, which name passes a property to the other?
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-eq-sym.hint.1: Q in the goal is an arbitrary property; P in the given can also represent a statement involving Q.
Here the given and the goal exchange the Morning Star and the Evening Star.
level.h-and-make.title: Defining with quantifiers
level.iffUse.intro.0.t: The iff declared in <level-ref to="decl-equiv"></level-ref> needs \mark{implies} both ways. Now reason from a given iff.
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-1.hint.0: Compare the sides of the given equivalence with the goal. Which side is the other given?
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-2.hint.0: Compare the negated given and the negated goal. Which side of the equivalence does each refer to?
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-subst.after: Equivalence substitution leaves the rest of the proved sentence in place.
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-subst.brief: Use Eq. substitution to replace \(A\) in \(\neg A\) with \(B\) and prove \(\neg B\).
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-subst.hint.0: Look at the selectable positions in the original sentence. Which part matches one side of the equivalence?
You just proved \(\neg B\) from \(\neg A\). Now look at how the equivalence relates to the \(A\) inside the original sentence.
level.iffUse.title: Prove iff
level.is-silent.intro.0.t: a says “b is a knave”. b stays silent. c says “a and b are the same kind”.
level.is-silent.tasks.is-silent.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the identities it can determine and reports failure for the rest.
level.is-silent.tasks.is-silent.hint.0: Not everyone’s kind can be settled.
level.is-silent.title: Missing facts
level.is-ten.after: The truth table for ten people has 1024 rows. Programs that decide problems like this are called SAT solvers, and they handle millions of variables.
level.is-ten.intro.0.t: Ten people stand in a ring. From a to i, each says the next person is a knave. j says “a and b are both knaves”.
level.is-ten.tasks.is-ten.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.is-ten.tasks.is-ten.hint.0: Compared with <level-ref to="is-three"></level-ref>, how many people’s statements must hold at once?
level.is-ten.title: Ten islanders
level.is-three.intro.0.t: a says “b is a knave”, b says “c is a knave”, and c says “a and b are both knaves”.
level.is-three.intro.1.t: In <level-ref to="e-three"></level-ref>, you wired these three statements into a circuit and ran all eight rows. In <level-ref to="kk-three"></level-ref>, you proved islanders’ identities by hand. This time, use a proof assistant for the three-person case.
level.is-three.tasks.is-three.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.is-three.title: Three identities
level.k.after: In a <wiki-ref to="hilbert"></wiki-ref>, which has no box, K is an <wiki-ref to="axiom"></wiki-ref>, taken without proof.
level.k.tasks.k-1.hint.0: What can be seen from inside the box?
level.k.tasks.k-2.hint.0: How many \mark{implies}s are in the goal?
level.k.tasks.k-2.hint.1: The inner box sees the outer box’s assumption.
level.k.tasks.k-2.intro.0.t: What holds still holds under any extra condition: windy or not, it rains. The sentence is called <part-ref to="lemma:axK"></part-ref>.
level.k.tasks.k-2.step: One more condition does no harm
level.k.title: Extra condition
level.kk-one.after: This is the island’s form of the <wiki-ref to="liar"></wiki-ref>.
level.kk-one.intro.0.t: Everyone on the island is a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies.
level.kk-one.intro.1.t: When an islander says something, “he is a knight” is in <wiki-ref to="equivalence"></wiki-ref> with what he says, written \mark{iff}. You translated this in <level-ref to="e-says"></level-ref>, and took \mark{iff} apart on the prover in <level-ref to="iffUse"></level-ref>.
level.kk-one.tasks.kk-one-1.brief: An islander a says: “I am a knave.” Wire it as a circuit: it outputs true on the rows where what a says fits what a is.
level.kk-one.tasks.kk-one-1.hint.0: Compare a’s identity with the identity he claims. When do they agree?
level.kk-one.tasks.kk-one-2.hint.0: What does each side of the given equivalence say?
level.kk-one.tasks.kk-one-2.hint.1: If a is a knight, what does his statement imply about his identity?
level.kk-one.tasks.kk-one-2.intro.0.t: Prove that nobody can say “I am a knave”: derive a contradiction from its translation.
level.kk-one.title: A claimed knave
level.kk-three.tasks.kk-three-1.brief: Two islanders, a and b; a says: “I am a knave, or b is a knight.” Wire it as a circuit: it outputs true on the rows where what a says fits what a is.

level.s-barbara.intro.0.t: Lewis Carroll, author of Alice in Wonderland, was a logician. He made many reasoning puzzles: a few sentences of “all”, “no” and “some”, from which a conclusion must be drawn.
level.s-barbara.intro.1.t: The simplest kind is Aristotle’s syllogism: “all A are B, all B are C, so all A are C”.
level.s-barbara.tasks.s-barbara.after: For over two thousand years the syllogism was nearly all of logic.
level.s-barbara.tasks.s-barbara.hint.0: Where do the three properties occur in the premises and conclusion?
level.s-barbara.tasks.s-carroll.hint.0: What relations do the three premises state between babies, being illogical, respect and taming crocodiles?
level.s-barbara.tasks.s-carroll.hint.1: Which premises mention respect, and how do they differ?
Carroll’s own puzzle: “babies are illogical”, “whoever can tame a crocodile is respected”, “illogical persons are not respected”. Prove “babies cannot tame crocodiles”.

level.s-equal.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="s-loop"></level-ref>, you made a search stop when it could not prove a goal. These cases include equations: some are givens, while another occurs in a goal. The last case is still expected to fail.

level.s-explore.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="s-append"></level-ref>, routes came together. Here the sentence matching a given is at different depths and positions in each goal, and the number of parts is limited. <part-ref to="part:search"></part-ref> can explore several routes.

level.s-explore.tasks.s-explore.hint.0: As it runs, watch where the result stops after a route fails.

level.s-loop.tasks.s-loop.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that follow and reports failure for the rest.

level.s.intro.0.t: When it rains, if it’s windy it’s wet; when it rains, it’s windy. So when it rains, it’s wet: Apply under the condition “it rains”. This sentence is called <part-ref to="lemma:axS"></part-ref>.

level.sp-nnf.after: Conjunctive normal form organises a sentence into clauses that an automated prover can process further.
level.sp-nnf.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="au-iff"></level-ref>, you proved another way to express equivalence. Now give sentences of different shapes a common form: in <wiki-ref to="nnf"></wiki-ref>, there is no \mark{iff} or \mark{implies}, and each \mark{not} applies to a smallest sentence.
level.sp-nnf.intro.1.t: Another form is <wiki-ref to="cnf"></wiki-ref>: it is also in negation normal form, with strings of “or” joined by “and”. Each string is a <wiki-ref to="clause"></wiki-ref>. In these cases, the connectives appear in different positions.
level.sp-nnf.tasks.sp-nnf-cnf.brief: Design a proof assistant that brings each goal to conjunctive normal form. The proof assistant you build becomes a new part, <part-ref to="lemma:cnf"></part-ref>.

level.sp-repeat.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="machine-cite-first"></level-ref>, one prover handled two cases. One could cite a given immediately, while the other had to unpack a conditional first. Here, one prover must again prove every case, but each case needs a different number of rewrites, and one needs none.
level.sp-repeat.intro.1.t: <part-ref to="part:repeat"></part-ref> keeps running the rewrite inside it until the proof state stops changing. The same automatic prover can then rewrite each case as many times as it needs and finish by citing a given.

level.sp-simp.tasks.sp-simp.brief: Design a proof assistant that rewrites each goal into the required form using the given equations and equivalences.

level.table.after: The forecast is false only if it rains and the ground stays dry. This reading of “if … then …” is called material implication.
level.table.intro.0.t: The forecast says, “If it rains, then it’s wet.” This statement can be true or false, so it is a proposition.
level.table.intro.1.t: “It rains” and “it’s wet” can each be true or false, giving four combinations. A <wiki-ref to="truth"></wiki-ref> records one combination per row and shows whether the whole forecast is true in that case.
level.table.intro.2.t: In “if X, then Y”, X is the antecedent and Y is the consequent. Here, “it rains” is the antecedent and “it’s wet” is the consequent.
level.table.tasks.table.brief: Use the rain and ground conditions in each row to mark “If it rains, then it’s wet” as true or false.
level.table.tasks.table.hint.0: In which case has the forecast got it wrong?
level.table.tasks.table.hint.1: On the two rows where it does not rain, has the forecast got it wrong?
level.table.title: Truth table
level.try-backtracking.after: A rule can apply even when the resulting goal cannot be proved. Join candidates preserves the other route, so Backtracking can return to it if the first route fails.
level.try-backtracking.intro.0.t: To prove “if it rains, it’s wet”, you can use an assumption box: add “it rains” to the givens, then try to prove “it’s wet”. If the full conditional is already a given, you can cite it directly.
level.try-backtracking.intro.1.t: Use Join candidates to send both routes to Backtracking. Try ① first. If it reaches a dead end, return to the fork and try ②. Switch the run report to the branch tree to see which path finishes the proof.
level.try-backtracking.tasks.try-backtra: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.

level.try-direct-backward.after: Each \mark{backward} card applies a proof rule directly to the current goal. Its output can feed the next tactic card.
level.try-direct-backward.intro.0.t: A card marked \mark{backward} takes a proof state directly. \mark{backward} Assume adds the condition of an implication to the givens. \mark{backward} Cite a given closes a goal that matches a given.
level.try-direct-backward.tasks.try-dire: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
Start with \mark{backward} Assume, then finish with \mark{backward} Cite a given.

level.try-direct-rewrite.after: The double-negation law can rewrite inside a formula. In these cases it removes the double negation and leaves the surrounding formula intact.

level.try-direct-rewrite.tasks.try-direc: Design a proof assistant that uses a rewrite card to remove the double negation in each goal.

level.try-or-elim.after: The elimination rule is \(\llbracket A\lor B;\ \llbracket A\rrbracket\Longrightarrow R;\ \llbracket B\rrbracket\Longrightarrow R\rrbracket\Longrightarrow R\). When the introduction rules describe all the ways to construct a proof, a case analysis rule can be generated from them. Each introduction rule gives one branch. Both branches reach the same R, so \(A\lor B\) is enough to use that case analysis.
level.try-or-elim.intro.0.t: Suppose a classmate will take the bus or the train. To show they can arrive by eight, consider each route. The same idea works for \(A\lor B\). To use it, consider the case where A holds and the case where B holds.
level.try-or-elim.intro.1.t: Or has two introduction rules. A proof of A gives \(A\lor B\), and so does a proof of B.
level.try-or-elim.tasks.try-or-elim.brie: R stands for any proposition. The premise \(A\lor B\) and conclusion R are fixed. Add two premises using the “assume … and derive …” card to show how each case leads to R.
level.try-or-elim.tasks.try-or-elim.hint: Assume A on one card and B on the other. Both cards must derive R.
level.try-or-elim.title: Or rule
level.try-rule-box.after: A test case can expose a difference between a rule and its intended behavior. An assumption box takes a proof under an assumption, so its conclusion alone does not describe the input.
level.try-rule-box.intro.0.t: Someone wrote the assumption-box rule as \(\llbracket B\rrbracket\Longrightarrow A\to B\). Use a test case to see whether it accepts the input you normally give the box.
level.try-rule-box.intro.1.t: A test case lists the input evidence, the conclusion you want, and the expected result. \(\llbracket A\rrbracket\Longrightarrow B\) means “assume A and derive B under that assumption.”
level.try-rule-box.tasks.try-rule-box.br: Edit the test case’s premise to give the assumption box an input it should accept. Run the test to find what the rule overlooks.
level.try-rule-box.tasks.try-rule-box.hi: Compare the premise on the rule board with the proof inside an assumption box. Which one shows the assumption?
level.try-rule-box.title: Rule check
level.try-rules.after: Apply takes a conditional and its condition to give its result. Chain combines two conditionals into one, ready for the next step.
level.try-rules.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="mergeUse"></level-ref>, you connected a proved result to another proof. A part receives premises at its inputs and gives a conclusion at its output. A rule is written \(\llbracket\text{premises}\rrbracket\Longrightarrow\text{conclusion}\). A, B, and C can stand for any propositions; each letter keeps the same meaning within a rule.
level.try-rules.intro.1.t: Select “Add a premise” for each input. Select the empty slot in “Conclusion” to enter the output, then select “Check”.
level.try-rules.tasks.try-rules-apply.br: Write the premises and conclusion of <part-ref to="part:mp"></part-ref> on the rule board.
level.try-rules.tasks.try-rules-apply.hi: The two inputs take \(A\to B\) and A. Which sentence comes out?
level.try-rules.tasks.try-rules-chain.br: Feed \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\) into <part-ref to="lemma:chain"></part-ref>. Write its premises and conclusion on the rule board.
level.try-rules.tasks.try-rules-chain.hi: Look at the two conditionals. How does the result of the first relate to the condition of the second?

level.twice.intro.0.t: “\(\text{it rains}\to (\text{it rains}\to \text{it’s wet})\)” states the condition “it rains” twice. Surely once is enough.

level.twice.tasks.twice.hint.1: How many times can an assumption in a box be used?

level.u-barber.after: This kind of argument is the <wiki-ref to="diagonal"></wiki-ref>.
level.u-barber.intro.0.t: When a goal follows, the saturator reaches \mark{bottom} sooner or later; when it does not, the saturator may never stop. level.u-cantor.after: This is Cantor’s theorem: a set always has more subsets than elements.

level.u-halt.after: Passing from one problem to another is a <wiki-ref to="reduction"></wiki-ref>. Provability in first-order logic shows the same <wiki-ref to="undecidable"></wiki-ref>: no program can say, for every goal, whether it follows.

part.arrow.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(A\to B\), gives \(\lnot A\lor B\); from \(\lnot A\lor B\), gives \(A\to B\).
part.arrow.name: Arrow away
part.arrow.revisions.0.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(A\to B\), gives \(\lnot A\lor B\); from \(\lnot A\lor B\), gives \(A\to B\). Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
part.auto.desc: Search automatically for a proof, returning the result if found and reporting failure if the search does not succeed.
part.auto.name: Your own auto
part.axK.desc: Choose two sentences \(A\) and \(B\) on the part; gives \(A \to (B \to A)\).
part.axK.settings.A.label: First
part.axK.settings.B.label: Second
part.axS.desc: Choose three sentences \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) on the part; gives \((A \to (B \to C)) \to ((A \to B) \to (A \to C))\).
part.axS.settings.A.label: First
part.axS.settings.B.label: Second
part.axS.settings.C.label: Third
part.botE.desc: From the contradiction \(\bot\), gives whatever sentence is chosen on the part.
part.botE.name: Explosion
part.botE.settings.C.label: Conclude
part.chain.desc: From \(A \to B\) and \(B \to C\), gives \(A \to C\).
part.chain.name: Chain
part.clausify.desc: Adds the negated goal to the hypotheses, brings them to CNF, removes the existential quantifiers and splits them into clauses.
part.clausify.name: Into clauses, all the way
part.cnf.desc: Brings sentences into conjunctive normal form.
part.cnf.name: CNF
part.cnf.settings.at.label: Where
part.cnf.settings.at.options.0.label: Goal
part.cnf.settings.at.options.1.label: Hypotheses
part.dist.desc: “Or” distributed over “and”, four shapes switched on the part: \(A\lor (B\land C)\) and \((A\lor B)\land (A\lor C)\) give each other, and so do \((A\land B)\lor C\) and \((A\lor C)\land (B\lor C)\).
part.dist.name: Distribute
part.dist.revisions.0.desc: “Or” distributed over “and”, four shapes switched on the part: \(A\lor (B\land C)\) and \((A\lor B)\land (A\lor C)\) give each other, and so do \((A\land B)\lor C\) and \((A\lor C)\land (B\lor C)\). Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
part.dm.desc: A negation trades “or” for “and” and back, four shapes switched on the part: \(\lnot (A\lor B)\) and \(\lnot A\land \lnot B\) give each other, and so do \(\lnot (A\land B)\) and \(\lnot A\lor \lnot B\).
part.dm.name: De Morgan
part.dm.revisions.0.desc: A negation trades “or” for “and”, “there is” for “for all”, and back: eight shapes switched on the part.
part.dneg.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(\lnot \lnot A\), gives \(A\); from \(A\), gives \(\lnot \lnot A\).
part.dneg.name: Double negation
part.dneg.revisions.0.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(\lnot \lnot A\), gives \(A\); from \(A\), gives \(\lnot \lnot A\). Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
part.each.desc: The parts inside run once on each goal, seeing only that goal each time; if any goal fails, the whole part fails.
part.each.name: Each goal
part.each.regions.0.label: Each goal
part.exE.desc: Connect \(\exists x.\, P(x)\); the box gives the existing thing a new name, such as \(a\). Inside the box, \(P(a)\) may be assumed. Prove \(C\) and connect it to “Conclusion” to obtain \(C\) outside. \(a\) must not appear in \(C\).
part.exE.name: Witness
part.exE.regions.0.label: Inside
part.exI.desc: Connect \(P(t)\) to obtain \(\exists x.\, P(x)\), with \(t\) as a witness. If exactly one existential statement fits, it is selected automatically; if several fit, choose the conclusion on the part.
part.exI.name: Generalise
part.exI.settings.target.label: Conclusion to derive
part.gAnd.desc: \(a \land b\): outputs true only when both inputs are true; otherwise false.
part.gAnd.name: And \mark{and}
part.gFalse.desc: Outputs false for every choice of inputs.
part.gFalse.name: Contradiction \mark{bottom}
part.gIff.desc: \(a \leftrightarrow b\): outputs true when \(a\) and \(b\) are both true or both false; false when one is true and the other false.
part.gIff.name: Equivalent \mark{iff}
part.gImp.desc: Outputs false only when \(a\) is true and \(b\) is false; true otherwise.
part.gImp.name: Implies \mark{implies}
part.gNot.desc: \(\lnot a\): true in gives false out; false in gives true out.
part.gNot.name: Not \mark{not}
part.gOr.desc: Outputs true when at least one input is true; false when both are false.
part.gOr.name: Or \mark{or}
part.gTrue.desc: Outputs true for every choice of inputs.
part.gTrue.name: Always True \mark{top}
part.gXor.desc: Outputs true when exactly one of its two inputs is true.
part.gXor.name: XOR \mark{xor}
part.iff.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(A\leftrightarrow B\), gives \((\lnot A\lor B)\land (\lnot B\lor A)\), and the other way round. Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
part.iff.name: Equivalence away
part.iffSubst.desc: Connect the equivalence and the original sentence. Choose a direction, then select one boxed subformula to replace it with the other side of the equivalence.
part.iffSubst.inputs.0.label: Equivalence
part.iffSubst.inputs.1.label: Original sentence
part.iffSubst.name: Eq. substitution
part.impI.desc: A box, with \(A\) set on the part. Inside, \(A\) may be used as an assumption; prove \(B\) there and wire it to “Conclusion”, and the part gives \(A \to B\).
part.impI.name: Assume
part.impI.regions.0.label: Inside
part.impI.settings.A.label: Assume
part.lem.desc: Choose a sentence \(A\) on the part; gives \(A \lor \lnot A\).
part.lem.name: Excluded middle
part.liar.name: The liar
part.merge.name: Merge
part.metis.desc: Turns the goal into clauses, finds a certificate that reaches \(\bot\) and has the kernel replay it: if it passes, the goal is closed; if the certificate fails the check, the part fails.
part.metis.name: Reconstructor
part.mp.name: Apply
part.mp.revisions.0.desc: From \(A \to B\) and \(A\), gives \(B\). \(\lnot A\) is \(A \to \bot\), so from \(\lnot A\) and \(A\), gives the contradiction \(\bot\).
part.orE.desc: Connect \(A \lor B\) and assume \(A\) and \(B\) in separate boxes. When both prove the same \(C\) and connect it to their respective “Conclusion” ports, the part outputs \(C\).
part.orE.name: Case analysis
part.orE.regions.0.label: Case one
part.orE.regions.1.label: Case two
part.orI.desc: Connect \(A\) and choose another statement \(B\) and its position to get \(A \lor B\) or \(B \lor A\). \(B\) need not be proved.
part.orI.name: Add alternative
part.orI.settings.other.label: Added disjunct
part.orI.settings.side.label: Position
part.orI.settings.side.options.0.label: Left
part.orI.settings.side.options.1.label: Right
part.oracle.desc: A fast prover: it cancels all complementary literals between two clauses at once, round after round until \(\bot\) appears or no new clause does. It too records the two parents of each new clause.
part.oracle.name: Someone else’s prover
part.raa.name: By contradiction
part.refl.desc: Choose a thing \(t\) on the part; gives \(t = t\).
part.refl.name: Reflexivity
part.refl.settings.t.label: Which thing
part.repeat.desc: Run the parts in the frame until the result stops changing. If a round fails, return the previous result. When there are several results, continue only with the first.
part.repeat.name: Repeat frame
part.repeat.regions.0.label: Each round
part.replay.desc: When the clause set contains \(\bot\), the steps to \(\bot\) go to the kernel: each input clause used must come from a hypothesis, and each step must be proved from its two parents (variables instantiated by unification) by Own auto. If all pass, the goal the clauses came from is proved; otherwise it names the failing step.
part.replay.name: Replay
part.res.desc: Wire in two clauses, one holding \(A\) and the other \(\lnot A\), in any position: that pair is cancelled and what is left is joined with “or”; when nothing is left, gives the contradiction \(\bot\). One pair at a time.
part.res.name: Resolve
part.resolve.desc: Tries every pair of clauses in the set once: when a literal of one unifies with the complement of a literal of the other, that pair is cancelled and the remaining literals form a new clause, added with a record of its two parents. Tautologies and duplicates are dropped. It can be set to resolve only against one-literal clauses.
part.resolve.name: Resolution round
part.resolve.settings.unit.label: Cancel with
part.rewrite.desc: Wire in \(s = t\) and a sentence containing \(s\); the part marks each \(s\) in it, and the ticked ones become \(t\).
part.rewrite.name: Substitute equals
part.rewrite.settings.at.label: Which occurrences to replace
part.saturate.desc: Resolves round after round until \(\bot\) appears or no new clause does.
part.saturate.name: The saturator
part.search.desc: Explore routes produced by the parts in the frame, following one route deeply before backtracking to others. The maximum number of layers can be set.
part.search.name: Backtracking search
part.search.regions.0.label: Each step
part.search.settings.depth.label: At most
part.simp.desc: Repeatedly rewrites using equations and equivalences among the givens until none applies.
part.simp.name: Simp
part.simp.settings.at.label: Where
part.simp.settings.at.options.0.label: Goal
part.simp.settings.at.options.1.label: Hypotheses
part.skolem.desc: Removes every \(\exists\) from the first goal’s hypotheses: one with no \(\forall\) outside is taken out as the instance box does; one under a \(\forall\) becomes a new function of all the enclosing \(\forall\) variables (\(sk1(x)\) …). The hypotheses must be in negation normal form first.
part.skolem.name: Skolemise
part.swap.name: Swap
part.toClauses.desc: The first goal must be \(\bot\): its hypotheses are split into clauses. Each must be in CNF; conjunctions are split, each disjunction becomes a clause, universal quantifiers are dropped and variables read as universally quantified.
part.toClauses.name: Extract clauses
